11	`env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh api /repos/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/<N> --jq '.parent.number'` **always
12	returns `null`**, whether or not the issue has a parent. The REST issue payload carries no `parent`
13	object — the field is **`parent_issue_url`**.
14	
15	So any "find the orphans" sweep written against `.parent` reports **every** issue as an orphan.
16	Verify parentage only via `.parent_issue_url`, or authoritatively via
17	`GET /repos/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/<parent>/sub_issues`. GraphQL's `parent` field does work, but
18	GraphQL times out on this repo often enough that REST is the usual path.

21	artifact of missing parentage, not completeness.** #989 (core) showed 12/12 closed and looked

23	rollup. After parenting it read 12/13 with one open child. **Always parent the orphans BEFORE

engine: implement the concrete WriteWavePublisher over the real seams
open
## Why this is not wiring

`WriteWavePublisher` (`crates/engine/src/rotation/rotate_write.rs`) is the write-plane rotation's transport edge. #1014 landed the two read-plane seams over the real network plane and deliberately stopped short of this one: three of its five methods are plumbing, but `republish` cannot be implemented against the seam as it stands.

Both blocking questions are now answered by **[ADR 0004 — Read-body child names are rewritten by the write-plane name wave](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/blob/main/decisions/0004-read-body-child-names-on-the-name-wave.md)** (FSM1/cipher-box-next#58, merged). **Read it before starting** — it settles a second, larger gap that this issue originally did not name.

## What the ADR settles

**D1 — the publisher re-resolves; it is not handed the authoring material.** The record handed to `republish` carries only routing identity:

```rust
pub struct RepublishedNode {
    pub node_id: [u8; 16],
    pub new_name: IpnsName,
    pub write_epoch: u64,
    pub is_root: bool,
}
```

Authoring at `new_name` additionally needs the node's read body, the read key it seals under, and the predecessor name. Widening this struct does not work as stated, because the orchestrator does not hold that material either — `WriteScopeNode` is `{node_id, current_name, child_node_ids}` — so it would mean widening `WriteSubtreeResolver` too, and dragging O(subtree) bodies and per-node key material through a primitive that currently holds exactly one secret.

Instead: add **`current_name: IpnsName`** to `RepublishedNode`, and let the concrete publisher do the gated read at `current_name` and author at `new_name`. This mirrors the landed read-plane precedent — `OwnerRotationNet::publish_scope_root` already does exactly this, and says so in code: *"The read body and the envelope fields a republish preserves come from the node's own current record, gated — the rotation carries neither."* The resume contract stays trivially intact: `is_republished(new_name)` is unchanged and still answers from published state alone.

**D2 — the read body cannot be carried verbatim.** `ChildRef.ipns_name` (`crates/core/src/seal/body.rs`) lives in the **read** body. The wave moves every node in the subtree to a freshly derived name, so afterwards every parent's child refs name nodes that have moved, and once interior old names batch-retire they name nothing.

Write-grantees are fine — they derive names from `writeScopeSeed`. **Read-only survivors cannot**: `open_grant_blob` returns `write_scope_seed: None` for a read-only grant, and the re-point object carries `currentRootName` and no other name. So without a rewrite, a read-only grantee reaches the new root and cannot descend. #26 D3's "read-only survivors follow republished mirrors" was pointing at exactly this and was never elaborated; the blueprint dropped the clause entirely.

So the wave **rewrites each `ChildRef.ipnsName`** to the child's freshly derived name and re-seals the read body under the node's unchanged read key at the unchanged read epoch. Child-first ordering already makes every child's new name known before its parent publishes.

## Scope

1. **Widen `RepublishedNode` with `current_name`** and update `rotate_scope_write`'s call site plus the simulation tests.
2. **Land the concrete `WriteWavePublisher`** over `RecordTransport` + `ApiClient`:
   - `register` / `retire` over `net::register` and `net::retire` — already bounded and idempotent, reuse rather than duplicate;
   - `is_republished` over the fan-out GET;
   - `republish` over the gated read at `current_name`, the read-body child-name rewrite, then `net::author` + `net::record_publish`, signing under `kdf::ipns_keypair(write_seed(freshWriteScopeSeed, node_id))`;
   - `publish_repoint` across the three channels — scope pointer, mailbox, old-root tombstone.
3. **Thread the read-plane material the rewrite needs** — the node's read key, and a nonce from the entropy seam. The read epoch must **not** move: a same-epoch rewrite is not a read rotation and must raise no read-epoch floor (#38 D1, each plane's clock authored by its own authority).
4. **Root linger stays**: `retire` must never include the old root name, and `root_retire_ready` is still stubbed `false` pending the migration-window constant.

## Definition of done

- [x] `blueprint/engine.md` `### rotateScopeWrite` and `blueprint/core.md`'s child-ref carve-out — **done in #1066**, so the blueprint is already normative for this work; read it, don't re-derive it
- [ ] `rotate_write.rs`'s module header narrowed: "The read plane is untouched" is true of keys, seeds and `minReadEpoch`, not of read-body bytes
- [ ] `RepublishedNode`'s doc comment stops promising a byte-stable republish with the read body carried verbatim
- [ ] ADR 0004 `Status:` flipped to `Accepted — implemented in FSM1/cipher-box#<this PR> (merged)` via a follow-up commit on cipher-box-next, per the ADR 0002 precedent

The blueprint is maintained **here**, not in cipher-box-next — that repo's `blueprint/` copies are the as-charted archive and must not be edited.

## Gate

- Resumed name waves via the write-plane history link, and crash recovery from published records only, per #635.
- Register-first ordering enforced **structurally**, so a publish of an unregistered name is impossible rather than merely unlikely.
- After a wave, a read-only holder starting from the re-pointed `currentRootName` resolves **every** node in the subtree — asserted at depth greater than one, so a root-only pass cannot satisfy it.
- Every republished parent's `ChildRef.ipnsName` set equals the derived new names of its children, and no retired name survives anywhere in the subtree's read bodies.
- The read epoch and every read-epoch floor are unchanged across the wave while the write epoch advances — the two planes' clocks stay independently authored.
- A resumed wave that skips already-republished nodes still leaves no stale child name behind.

6

The two cannot simply be sequenced either: the new root name only exists after `rotate_scope_write` mints the fresh write scope seed, so #1019's cut and this rotation need a decided seam between them.

**Title:** `engine: two of the three re-point channels never publish, so a lagging reader has only the scope pointer`
**Parent:** #635 · **blocked_by:** none · **blocks:** #1019

`WriteWavePublisher::publish_repoint` returns `WritePublishError::NotLanded` for both `RepointChannel::Mailbox` and `RepointChannel::Tombstone` (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:1495-1502`). Neither channel has a wire shape: no tombstone record type, author or decoder exists in `crates/engine`, and `mailbox::post_sealed` seals internally, so a pre-sealed re-point block would double-seal into a format nothing opens. The blueprint specifies all three (`blueprint/engine.md` "rotateScopeWrite", #38 D3), and the accelerators are what let a surviving grantee learn of a re-point before its next pointer consult. The wave completes without them, so this is a latency and discovery defect rather than a safety one, but it must be honest before a production caller ships. **Title:** `engine: the scope pointer record never renews, so the only landed re-point channel lapses at its EOL`
**Parent:** #635 · **blocked_by:** none · **blocks:** #1019 · **relates to:** #1043 (the same defect for the vault settings record)

`publish_scope_pointer` (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:1349-1385`) publishes the canonical re-point and never enrols the pointer name in the held set, so `keyless_re_put` and `eol_renew_pass` (`crates/engine/src/net/liveness.rs:109`, `:225`) never see it and the record dies at its 90-day client-signed EOL. **Title:** `engine: the old root name lingers forever because the migration-window constant does not exist`

The current direction is the fail-safe one, so this is quota accretion, not a trust defect.

## Problem

`WriteWaveNet::publish_scope_pointer` (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:1349`) publishes the scope pointer through `publish_inline` and then advances the sequence floor. It never enrols the pointer name in the held set, so neither `keyless_re_put` nor `eol_renew_pass` (`crates/engine/src/net/liveness.rs:105`, `:225`) ever sees it.

The pointer therefore dies at its 90-day client-signed EOL. The API republisher is keyless by design and cannot extend a client-signed validity, so nothing renews it.

## Why it matters

The scope pointer is the **canonical** re-point channel. `publish_repoint` (`net/rotation.rs:1487`) returns `NotLanded` for both `RepointChannel::Mailbox` and `RepointChannel::Tombstone`, so the pointer is currently the only landed channel a read-only survivor has.

A read-only grantee cannot derive the new root name — `open_grant_blob` returns `write_scope_seed: None` for a read-only grant. It learns the new root only by consulting the pointer. Once the pointer's EOL lapses, a cold-starting survivor cannot find the new root at all, and the loss is silent: an unresolvable name is indistinguishable from a name that never existed.

## Complication

`HeldRecord.head_cid` (`liveness.rs:63`) is a required `/ipfs/` head, and a held record with an empty head CID is skipped at `liveness.rs:245`. The pointer's `Value` is the sealed block inline, not a head CID. So the held-set shape cannot carry an inline record as it stands.

## Proposed fix

Give `HeldRecord` an inline-or-head value shape, and enrol the scope pointer at publish time. Keep the release-active empty-head guard for the head variant.

Related: #1043 is the same defect for the vault settings record.

## 2. Evidence chain

**The binding is real, and it is the moving name.**

- `crates/core/src/kdf/mod.rs:285-289` — `blinded_tag(ecdh_shared, scope_root_ipns_name)`.
- `crates/engine/src/grants/ledger.rs:120` — `mint_grant_row` derives both the commitment entry tag and the ledger row tag from that call.
- `CONTEXT.md:26` — "A node's Ed25519 IPNS keypair, its `ipnsName`, and its `writeKey` all derive from its write seed." There is **one** name per node, and it is the write-plane name. There is no separate stable read-plane name. The dissolution path in the question is closed.
- `crates/engine/src/grants/create.rs:302` — the owner mints the grant at `derive_write_name(grantee.write_scope_seed, &grantee.scope_id)`, i.e. the write-plane name, never a stable identifier.
- Executed: `crates/engine/src/grants/invite.rs:1034` `the_blinded_tag_binds_the_derived_scope_root_name` — same scope id, two different `write_scope_seed` values, `assert_ne!(here.tag, elsewhere.tag)`. **Passes** (`cargo test -p cipherbox-engine --lib grants::`, 77 passed).

**What the wave does to the grant section.**

- `crates/engine/src/rotation/rotate_write.rs:509`, `:529` — every node, root included, republishes at `derive_write_name(&write_scope_seed, node_id)` off a freshly minted random seed (`:486-495`).
- `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:1202-1206` — `reseal_root` clones the resolved commitment, overwrites **only** `ipns_name` with `node.new_name`, and owner-re-signs. `entries` (and therefore every `tag`) is cloned verbatim.
- `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:1231` — `grant_ledger: &plane.write_body.grant_ledger`, carried verbatim from the record resolved at the old name.
- `crates/engine/src/rotation/reseal.rs:356` — the blob loop re-seals fresh HPKE ciphertext but files it under `tag: entry.tag`, taken straight off the carried ledger row. `reseal.rs:353` signs the structure over that same stale tag.
- `crates/engine/src/rotation/reseal.rs:308` — the only consistency check is `enforce_committed_ledger`, which compares commitment-tags against ledger-tags. Both sides are stale in the same way, so it passes. Nothing anywhere compares a tag against the `ipns_name` it is supposed to bind.
- No occurrence of `blinded_tag`, `mint_grant_row`, or `recipient_blinded_tag` anywhere in `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs` or `crates/engine/src/rotation/`.

**The read side has no way to distinguish this from a revocation.**

- `crates/engine/src/gate/adoption.rs:547` — a record is rejected unless `section.commitment.ipns_name == candidate.name`. So the moved root's own owner-signed commitment asserts the **new** name. That is the only name the record self-describes with.
- `crates/engine/src/grants/ledger.rs:63-68` — `self_locate` is a plain tag equality scan.

## Problem

`reseal_scope_root` seals each grant blob to `entry.recipient_enc_pk` taken straight from the resolved write-body ledger, with no re-derivation of the tag it is filed under (`crates/engine/src/rotation/reseal.rs`, the grant-blob loop).

So a write-grantee that swaps a victim's `recipientEncPk` makes every subsequent honest re-seal — the owner's included — wrap the scope seed to the attacker's key under the victim's owner-committed tag. Owner authority passes at every step, and the victim simply stops being able to open its blob.

## Fix

The owner (and any re-sealer holding the owner encryption subkey) can re-derive the tag cheaply and refuse a row whose `recipientEncPk` does not produce the tag it is filed under. `crates/engine/src/grants/invite.rs`'s `convert_invite_claim` already does exactly this check against a recorded link:

```rust
let link_enc = X25519Public::from_bytes(link.ephemeral_enc_pk).ok_or(...)?;
if recipient_blinded_tag(owner.enc_secret, &link_enc, name) != Some(link.tag) { ... }
```

A re-sealer that is a write-grantee rather than the owner holds no owner encryption subkey and cannot run it, so the check has to be conditional on the material available — which is also the honest statement of the residual that remains.

## Gate

Rotation simulation: a re-seal over a ledger whose `recipientEncPk` was swapped under a committed tag must fail closed rather than wrap the seed to the swapped key, when the re-sealer holds the owner encryption subkey.

## Origin

Found by the `/crypto-privacy-review` gate on the grant-invite claim PR. Out of that PR's file ownership (`crates/engine/src/rotation/` belonged to a sibling slice), and strictly more severe than the in-diff residual it was found next to.

Design is clear, and the two fixes compose so that one proves the other:

- **#1135** — `reseal_root` re-mints each ledger row at the new root name before it re-seals, using `mint_grant_row(owner_enc_secret, identity_pk, enc_pk, scope_id, new_name, permission)`, which returns the tag, the commitment entry, and the ledger row together so they cannot drift apart.

On `ScopeRootIdentity` as `owner_enc_secret: Option<&'a X25519Secret>`, not on `CommittedSet`:

- `the_wave_refuses_a_ledger_row_the_commitment_does_not_commit_release_active`

content.text:
PR #1141 is up as a draft: 18 files, +721/−31, two commits, mergeable. I fixed the hygiene on the two issues it spun off — both were orphaned with only a `v2-build` label. #1142 now sits under #989 core with `comp:core`, #1143 under #635 with `comp:engine`, both on milestone v2.0.0. Their `blocked_by #1127` edges are right: #1127 closes when this merges, and they become actionable then.

I read the core change rather than taking the report on trust. `remint_grants` does the right things in the right order:

1. `enforce_committed_ledger` **first**, so a write-grantee cannot launder a self-upgraded row into a commitment the owner then signs.
2. Each row's tag must bind at the **old** name, which is what catches a swapped `recipientEncPk`.
3. Re-mint at the new name via `mint_grant_row`.
4. The re-minted `pseudonymPk` must equal the committed one — it binds the scope, not the name, and it authorizes structure signing.
5. `expires_at` and `unknown` carried forward on both the entry and the ledger row.
6. Sorted by tag, not by the order a write-grantee authored.

Then `reseal_root` passes `owner_enc_secret: Some(...)` into `reseal_scope_root` at the **new** name, so #1127's check re-validates the re-mint it just did. The tautology-at-the-mint-site property holds as designed.

`cargo fmt --all -- --check` exits 0 on my own run. The workspace test run is still going; I am re-running it independently rather than relying on the report.

Three findings from the implementation that I did not anticipate and that you should weigh:

- **#1143** — fail-closed hands a committed write-grantee a veto over its own revocation. One poisoned row now aborts the write wave and the read cascade, which are exactly the rotations that cut the attacker. #1127 specifies fail-closed and that is what shipped, but the availability trade was never weighed when the issue was written.
- **#1142** — the new check pins only the cofactor equivalence class of `recipientEncPk`. `blinded_tag` mixes the shared secret, not the key bytes, and `X25519Public::from_bytes` has no prime-order check, so a cofactor twin passes the binding while breaking DHKEM's `kem_context`. The victim stays locked out across the owner's rotation. That fix belongs in `crates/core`.
- `sweep_pass` is reached from `create_read_grant`, which **does** hold the owner subkey, so the same descendants get checked on one leg and unchecked on the other. Noted in #1143 rather than widened in this PR.

I will confirm the test result, then decide whether the review gates need a second pass given the two commits.

Do an independent cryptographic and trust-boundary review of PR #1141 in /Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box. The branch `fix/rotation-grant-tag-remint` is checked out at `58bdf82b0`. Review the full diff: `git diff origin/main...HEAD`.

Run gh as `env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh ...`. `gh issue view` is broken repo-wide; read issues via `env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh api /repos/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/<N> --jq '.body'`.

## Read-only

Report findings. Do not edit any file, do not commit, do not push, do not touch the PR or any issue.

## What the PR does

It fixes two linked defects:

- **#1135** — `kdf::blinded_tag(ecdh_shared, scope_root_ipns_name)` binds the scope root's `ipnsName`. A write rotation moves that name by construction. `WriteWaveNet::reseal_root` used to rewrite `commitment.ipns_name` and owner-re-sign it while cloning `commitment.entries` and passing the resolved `grant_ledger` through verbatim, so every grant blob stayed filed under a tag bound to the retired name. A surviving grantee re-derived its tag from the new name, missed, and `grants::revocation::classify` reads that as the definitive revocation signal. One write revoke read as a mass read-revoke.
- **#1127** — `reseal_scope_root` trusted `entry.recipient_enc_pk` verbatim, so a write-grantee that swapped a victim's `recipientEncPk` under the victim's owner-committed tag redirected every future honest re-seal.

The fix: `WriteWaveNet::remint_grants` (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs`) re-mints every row at the new name via `mint_grant_row`, and `reseal_scope_root` gained `ScopeRootIdentity::owner_enc_secret: Option<&X25519Secret>` — when `Some`, every ledger row must satisfy `recipient_blinded_tag(owner_enc_secret, recipient_enc_pub, identity.ipns_name) == Some(entry.tag)` before anything is sealed. On the write-wave path that check re-validates the re-mint that just happened.

## Focus your effort here

1. **Commit 2 (`58bdf82b0`, "pin the re-minted commitment to what the owner already signed") has never been reviewed.** It landed in response to the first review pass. Review it hardest. `git show 58bdf82b0`.
2. **`remint_grants` ordering.** It calls `enforce_committed_ledger` first, then checks each row's tag binds at the **old** name, then re-mints at the new name, then requires the re-minted `pseudonymPk` to equal the committed one. Is that ordering sufficient? Can a committed write-grantee still get something of its own choosing under the owner's fresh signature? The owner re-signs the commitment it builds from a ledger that a write-grantee authored — that is the laundering surface.
3. **Carried-forward fields.** `expires_at` and `unknown` are copied from the old entry onto the re-minted one on both the commitment entry and the ledger row. Can a write-grantee use `unknown` (preserved fields) or `expires_at` as a channel, given the owner now signs the result?
4. **The `None` path.** A write-grantee re-sealer passes `None` and skips the binding check entirely. Confirm that residual is stated honestly in the doc comments and that no production caller that *does* hold the owner subkey passes `None` by accident. Check every call site.
5. **Rule 8 symmetry.** Every new refusal must be release-active and return `Err`. Confirm no `debug_assert!`/`assert!` guards a trust check.
6. **Zeroization.** `X25519Secret` now threads through `ScopeRootIdentity`. Confirm the terminal-owner rule holds — a callee must not zero a caller-owned buffer, and secrets must not leak into `Debug`, logs, or error text.
7. **Sorting.** `remint_grants` sorts entries and ledger by tag. Confirm that is a genuine ordering-leak fix and that it cannot drop or merge rows (for example on a duplicate tag).
8. **Test honesty.** Seven new tests are claimed. Check they assert behavior and not source text, and that the ones described as release-active genuinely are. Look for a test that would pass whether or not the guard exists.

## Known and already-filed — do not re-report as new

- **#1142** — the check pins only the cofactor equivalence class of `recipientEncPk`, because `blinded_tag` mixes the shared secret and `X25519Public::from_bytes` has no prime-order check. Fix belongs in `crates/core`.
- **#1143** — fail-closed lets one poisoned row veto the write wave and the read cascade, the rotations that cut the attacker. Also that `sweep_pass` is reached from `create_read_grant`, which holds the owner subkey, so descendants are checked on one leg and unchecked on the other.
- The owner-root test fixture seals under a fixed key and nonce by blueprint design, so fixture variants sharing a `root_id` share a `(key, nonce)`. Test-corpus only.

If you find a **new** instance or a reason one of the above is worse than recorded, say so.

## Report back — the only thing I see

For each finding: severity (Critical / High / Medium / Low), the file:line, the concrete attack or failure sequence, and the minimal fix. Separate CONFIRMED findings from SPECULATIVE ones. If the PR is sound, say so plainly — do not manufacture findings.

End with a one-line verdict: is this safe to take out of draft and put in front of CodeRabbit and Greptile?

Write prose in Simplified Technical English: short active sentences, active voice, no contractions, no idioms.

### [Medium] The owner holds the subkey at `create_read_grant` step 6 and still re-seals the parent unchecked

**Location:** `/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box/crates/engine/src/grants/create.rs:470-476` (uses `&parent.identity`); plan field at `create.rs:125`; every construction passes `None` — `create.rs:783`, `create.rs:893`, `/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box/crates/contract/tests/contract.rs:1231`.

The PR added `owner_enc_secret: Some(owner.enc_secret)` at two of the three `reseal_scope_root` sites inside `create_read_grant` (`create.rs:342`, `create.rs:405`). The third, step 6's parent index update, uses `&parent.identity`, a whole `ScopeRootIdentity` handed in by the caller, and every construction in the tree sets `None`. `owner.enc_secret` is in scope at that line.

Attack: a committed write grantee of the **parent** scope re-authors the parent write body and replaces a victim's `recipientEncPk` under the victim's owner-committed tag. Permission and tag still match, so `enforce_committed_ledger` passes. The next `create_read_grant` — an owner action — re-seals the parent and wraps the parent's `override_seed` and `pointer_read_key` to the attacker's key (`rotation/reseal.rs:357-387`). That is #1127 verbatim, on the leg the PR edited and did not close.

Minimal fix: do not let a caller decide this. Drop `owner_enc_secret` from `ParentScopePlan::identity` and have `create_read_grant` build the parent identity with `Some(owner.enc_secret)`, as it already does for the grantee root and each descendant.

### [Medium] The re-mint turns an unauthenticated, unused ledger field into a free veto on the write wave

**Location:** `/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box/crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:1232-1233`

```rust
let recipient_identity = EcdsaVerifier::from_sec1(&entry.recipient_identity_pk)
    .ok_or(WritePublishError::Rejected)?;
```

`recipient_identity_pk` participates in no derivation. `mint_grant_row` only echoes it back (`grants/ledger.rs:146`), the commitment does not cover it (`enforce_committed_ledger` compares `(tag, permission)` only), and no authorization path reads it — the invite claim path matches on the owner-local `RecordedInvite.ephemeral_identity_pk` and the re-derived tag (`grants/invite.rs:517-529`), and `SentIndex` is owner-local (`grants/accept.rs:280-289`).

So a committed write grantee sets a victim's `recipientIdentityPk` to any 33 bytes that are not a curve point. `from_sec1` returns `None`, `remint_grants` returns `Rejected`, and the write wave — the operation that revokes that grantee — fails permanently, with no other symptom and no other check able to observe the field. `main` never parsed the field, so the lever is new in this PR. This is the #1143 mechanism, but with an attacker cost of zero and a fix that is local.

Minimal fix: carry the field verbatim as `expires_at` already is, rather than parsing a value nothing binds — either take the raw SEC1 bytes in `mint_grant_row`, or overwrite `ledger_entry.recipient_identity_pk = entry.recipient_identity_pk` after the mint and stop treating a parse failure as a trust verdict.

**Location:** guard at `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:1251-1253`; test at `rotation.rs:3672`

`the_re_mint_reproduces_the_committed_pseudonym_key` runs on honestly minted rows, so the mint reproduces the committed key by construction. Delete the guard and the test still passes. It asserts an invariant, not the refusal.

The same test's second assertion is **not** vacuous: I computed the fixture's two blinded tags at the post-wave name (`read[0]=0xe2`, `write[0]=0x76`), and the ledger order is `[read, write]`, so without the sort `is_sorted_by_key` fails. Minimal fix: one fixture with `rows[0].commitment_entry.pseudonym_pk = [0xaa; 32]` (owner still signs the commitment, tag left honest), asserting `Err(Rejected)` and `!published_at`.

TITLE: fix: expand pruned roots to their leaves and plan reclaim in pinned bytes
---
Three correctness defects on the prune path, all in `crates/engine/src/content/retention.rs`.

## \#849 — a root-only retire orphans every sealed leaf

`plan_prune` emitted root content CIDs only, but `POST /registry/retire` deletes rows for exactly the CIDs handed to it and never interprets content — it is zero-knowledge and cannot expand a root. Retiring a version therefore dropped the root's pin row and left every sealed leaf pinned and charged forever, while `reclaimed_bytes` reported the whole version freed. At the frozen 1 MiB framing any file over one chunk has more leaf bytes than root bytes, so this was the normal case.

New `expand_retire_targets(version, root_block)`. The root block is plaintext deterministic CBOR, so the leaf list is readable by CID alone with no key and no wire-format change.

- **Fail-closed throughout.** The block is refused past `MAX_RESOLVED_RECORD_BYTES` before it is hashed, then verified against the version's `contentCid` through `decode_content_cid_str` + `is_plane_anchor` + `verify_cid` — the same spelling `read.rs` and `staging.rs` already use, so the trust failure carries core's `TrustViolation::ContentCidMismatch` and an off-plane root CID is refused as malformed rather than conflated with a substituted block.
- **The walk is one level.** `decode_root` already enforces that every link is a `raw`-codec CID, and a raw block names no further links.
- **Leaves first, root last.** The root block is the only record of its own leaf list, so retiring it first would make those leaves unnameable and charged forever — exactly the defect, made permanent instead of transient. A drain that dies mid-expansion can always re-expand from a root that is still pinned.

`plan_prune` still emits roots only; the expansion is the drain-time step, matching the ledger-stores-roots decision in \#872. The API needed no change: the existing `retire` already takes an advisory lock on every path, bulk-deletes via `In(targets)`, and refcounts before unpinning, which is exactly right once the client hands it the full set.

## \#850 — plaintext bytes in a field meaning pinned bytes

`ContentVersion.size_bytes` was documented as the pinned size but was fed from `Version.size`, which is plaintext. Sealing adds 40 B per leaf plus the root block, and pinned bytes are what the registry charges, so the figure understated every reclaim and every quota pre-flight.

The field is now `pinned_bytes`, and `ContentVersion::from_plaintext_size(cid, plaintext_bytes, profile)` is the conversion — explicit at the boundary rather than implicit in an assignment, and it takes the framing profile because plaintext cannot be converted without it. It reuses the existing `sealed_total_bytes`, which derives the total from the leaf count and root-block length and is already held to real staging byte-for-byte.

The two figures are then bound **at runtime, not just in a test**: `expand_retire_targets` refuses unless the manifest's own leaf count and actual root-block length account for exactly the pinned total the plan quoted. That is \#872's acceptance criterion "`reclaimed_bytes` equals the sum of the sizes the retire call actually frees, in pinned bytes", enforced rather than asserted — and it closes the manifest's freedom to declare an arbitrary `size`/`chunkSize` pair, since those now have to reproduce the planned figure.

## \#851 — `keep_latest` admitted zero

`plan_prune` took a plain `usize`, so `skip(0)` yielded the whole history including the live version the file record still points at. It now takes `NonZeroU64`, making the state unrepresentable rather than guarded, and matching the `RetentionPolicy::KeepLatest(NonZeroU64)` the call site already holds — no lossy conversion at the boundary. The enum was already correct and is untouched. A keep-count past `usize` on a 32-bit target (wasm32 is a shipped target) clamps to keeping everything.

## Gate

`Engine Tests`. Fifteen unit tests in `crates/engine/src/content/retention.rs`, all behavioral. The fail-closed checks return `Err` rather than asserting, and the suite is verified green under `cargo test --release` so no check is compiled out.

`a_gibibyte_version_expands_past_one_retire_batch_with_the_root_last` pins the shape constraint: at the frozen framing a 1 GiB version expands to 1025 targets, past `REGISTRY_BATCH_MAX = 1000`, and the root still lands in the final batch after every leaf it names.

## Review gates

`/simplify`, `/security-review` and `/crypto-privacy-review` all ran on `git diff main...HEAD`. Folded in: routing the address check through the existing core primitives instead of a bespoke multibase string compare; binding the drain-time pinned total to the plan (which collapsed a `RetireExpansion` struct into a plain target list); removing an invariant restated on four call sites and an absence-justifying comment about recursion the function does not do; deleting a doc claim that a constructor was the only way to build a struct with public fields; a redundant test folded into its neighbour; and `with_capacity` instead of a `collect`-then-`push` realloc.

########## 1043 ##########
engine: the vault settings record never renews, so its EOL lapses on its own
---
PR for #904 lands an EOL check on the vault settings resolve — the one record whose reader is always its own signer, so refusing a lapsed one strands nobody (`blueprint/engine.md` "Vault settings load").

The refusal has no renewal behind it.

## The gap

Sub-EOL renewal runs over the **held set** only — `eol_renew_pass(..., held: &[HeldRecord])` in `crates/engine/src/net/liveness.rs`. `publish_settings` mints no `HeldRecord` and has no facade wiring at all, so the settings name never enters that set. The API republisher is keyless: it re-PUTs the same signed bytes and cannot extend a client-signed validity.

So an account whose settings have not been re-saved inside the 90-day window lapses on its own, with no adversary involved:

- a device with a warm cache pins to last-known-good indefinitely and reports `DefaultsReason::Expired`;
- a device without one — fresh install, evicted cache, second device — gets `SettingsLoad::Defaults(Expired)`, and the placement decision then fails closed for want of a copy it can authenticate.

That is availability, not a placement widening: the settings-load policy already says any reason other than `NoRecord` with no cached copy refuses the hosted upload rather than resolving to `PinMode::Hosted`. But it is a 90-day cliff on a timer.

## Resolving

Register the settings name in the held set at publish, so the existing `eol_renew_pass` covers it:

```rust
// publish_settings, after the confirmed outcome
let held = HeldRecord { routing_key: name.as_str().to_owned(), record_bytes, signer, head_cid: head.cid().to_owned(), content_cids: Vec::new() };
```

A seq+1 renewal republishes the same body, hence the same body revision, and the readers bar is strict `<` — so renewal is already compatible with the revision check that landed alongside the EOL one.

This belongs with the slice that wires the settings plane into the facade: `publish_settings` and `load_settings` have no production caller today, only the `crates/engine/tests/vault_settings.rs` suite, so there is nowhere to put the held-set insert yet.

########## 850 ##########
engine: ContentVersion.size_bytes conflates plaintext size with pinned size
---
## Problem

Two fields that flow into each other measure different things:

- `Version.size` is documented as **plaintext** bytes — "The plaintext size in bytes" (`crates/core/src/seal/body.rs:144-145`).
- `ContentVersion.size_bytes` is documented as the **pinned** size — "The version's pinned size in bytes (what a prune reclaims)" (`crates/engine/src/content/retention.rs:53-54`).

The prune path reads the version history out of `ReadBody::File { versions }` (`body.rs:246`) and maps it into `ContentVersion`, so the plaintext number lands in a field that means pinned bytes. `plan_prune` then sums it into `reclaimed_bytes` (`retention.rs:81`) and reports it to the user.

## The gap

Sealed bytes exceed plaintext by a fixed, computable amount:

- 40 B per leaf — a 24-byte XChaCha20-Poly1305 nonce plus a 16-byte tag (`crates/engine/src/content/chunk.rs:65,93`)
- plus the DAG root block itself: 41 B fixed + 38 B per inlined leaf CID

At the #820-frozen framing (`chunk_size = 1_048_536`, sealed leaf exactly 1 MiB) that is 78 B per chunk, so the under-report is small in ratio but always present and always in the same direction: **`reclaimed_bytes` understates what is actually freed**, on top of the much larger overstatement from the root-only retire defect. The two errors are independent and point opposite ways, so neither masks the other reliably.

The same conflation reaches the quota pre-flight: #822 §5 ruled the pre-flight must be sized in **sealed** bytes, because sealed bytes are what `registerPin` charges (`apps/api/src/content/content.service.ts:275`). Quoting plaintext under-reports every time.

## Fix

Pick one unit per field and make the conversion explicit at the boundary rather than implicit in an assignment. Derive the pinned total from the leaf count and root size rather than reusing the plaintext number, and add a test asserting `reclaimed_bytes` equals the sum of the sizes the retire call actually frees.

Found while resolving #820.

Closed by slice #872.

Part of #655


########## 872 ##########
engine: prune old versions and reclaim their bytes
---
Prune drops old file versions and reclaims their bytes. Prune is a **write-plane mutation** — it re-seals and publishes a shortened history — which is why #820 pulled it into this chain. Slice settled by #825 on wayfinder map #813.

## Scope

**This issue absorbs #849, #850 and #851 outright.** They were previously named as prerequisites in prose only, with no dependency edge, which made #872 look startable when it is not — and made three defects look like three shippable PRs. They are not: `plan_prune` (`crates/engine/src/content/retention.rs:93`) has **zero production callers** at `main` @ `3d087d673`. Its only references are the re-exports at `crates/engine/src/lib.rs:54` and `crates/engine/src/content/mod.rs:38`, and its own unit tests in `retention.rs`. Nothing reaches it, so none of the three is independently observable or independently testable end-to-end. Close all three as folded-in when this ships. Native `blocked_by` edges are recorded on this issue so the graph stays honest until they are.

**Three correctness fixes, folded in.**

- **#849 — leaf expansion.** `plan_prune` emits root content CIDs only, and `POST /registry/retire` deletes rows for exactly the CIDs handed to it without walking the DAG, so every sealed leaf stays pinned and charged forever while `reclaimed_bytes` reports the whole version freed. Expand each doomed root to `root + leaf_cids` before retiring, by fetching the root block and `decode_root`-ing it — the root block is plaintext det-CBOR, so no key is needed. Two constraints on its shape: `root + leaf_cids` **cannot be one call** — the registry batch cap is `REGISTRY_BATCH_MAX = 1000` (`crates/engine/src/net/mod.rs:25`), enforced by the chunking at `crates/engine/src/net/retire.rs:100`, and a 1 GiB version is 1025 targets at the frozen 1 MiB framing, so partial retire is normal at exactly `max_file_bytes` — and **leaves retire before their root**.
- **#850 — unit mismatch.** `ContentVersion.size_bytes` (`crates/engine/src/content/retention.rs:75`) is documented as the **pinned** size, but the prune path fills it from `Version.size`, which is **plaintext** bytes. The gap is fixed and computable (40 B per sealed leaf, plus the root block). A pending-reclaim total built on the wrong unit is the same misreport in a new place. Derive the pinned total from the leaf count and root size rather than reusing the plaintext number.
- **#851 — partially already fixed; check before you write.** The ticket claimed `keep_latest` admits zero at `retention.rs:72-73`. That is stale in two ways. `RetentionPolicy::KeepLatest(NonZeroU64)` **already exists** (`crates/engine/src/content/retention.rs:65`), with the doc stating the zero state is unrepresentable rather than guarded. The hole survives only on the free function: `plan_prune(versions_newest_first: &[ContentVersion], keep_latest: usize)` at `retention.rs:93` still takes a plain `usize` and `skip(0)` still yields the whole history including the live version. Close that one signature; do not re-do the enum.

**One op that ends at publish, plus a retire ledger that is not an op** (#852). Both alternatives put a garbage-collection call on the critical path of user work: one op with two legs holds the FIFO head so the next rename waits on cleanup, and two ops repeats that plus a sixth `OpKind` with vacuous rebase semantics.

**The ledger stores roots; leaves are re-derived** at drain time via `decode_root` — plaintext det-CBOR, no key. That is three orders of magnitude smaller, and it is the irrecoverable half: once the publish lands nothing readable references the dropped roots, while leaves always can be recovered from a root.

**Leaves before root, versions oldest-first.** The journaled root **is** the expansion key, so retiring it first makes its leaf list unnameable and those bytes charged forever. Oldest-first is what `plan_prune` already emits — `PrunePlan.retire_targets` is documented "oldest first" (`content/retention.rs:82`) and the plan is built by iterating the doomed suffix in reverse (`content/retention.rs:99-103`) — and it leaves a valid suffix of history. Together these make the drain resumable across restart with nothing journaled but roots.

**Entries clear only on the server's own done-signal** — a batch reporting `retired: 0`, which is positive evidence and also covers the succeeded-but-response-lost case. Everything else backs off forever: **no attempt budget, no gave-up list, no dead-letter class.** Every failure is either self-clearing (offline, 401, a 429 from the registry throttle, a 503 from lock contention) or ours (a 400 from a bad CID we emitted, an unfetchable root we are charging for), and in every case the only user action is `Command::ManualRefresh`, which already exists.

**Owed bytes ride the entry** as one `u64` from `ContentVersion.size_bytes` — in the corrected pinned unit, per the folded-in #850 — and surface as a **vault-level pending-reclaim figure** beside the quota, the ticket's own missing "record of what was owed".

**Mode-derived legs, bytes tracking hosted.** Hosted to hosted, External to provider, Dual to both; the byte figure drains on hosted confirmation. External accounts hold **size-zero rows** (`register()` records membership at size 0, hosted ingress refused for BYO, `content.service.ts:246-253`), so a hosted-only ledger would self-satisfy instantly in External mode.

**A distinct `RetireLedger` seam** with its own conformance kit, on `FloorStore`'s precedent. It diverges from the op queue on lifetime, ordering (a set, not a FIFO), failure contract (never-discard versus dead-letter) and cancellability at once. Reusing the op queue is cheaper and inherits #832's owner tag free, but it puts a non-FIFO non-cancellable record in a store whose cold-start sweep **deletes** what it cannot decode.

**Owner-scoping is forced, not tidy.** Account A's owed CIDs retried under account B's token delete no rows, return `retired: 0`, and satisfy the done-signal without reclaiming anything.

## Harvest reference

`apps/api/src/ipfs/pending-unpin/` on branch `v1` is the same shape server-side: a durable outbox drained in ordered batches, per-row failure isolation ("leave row for next run; do not abort the batch"), a refcount-then-unpin helper, and a depth gauge. v1 could place it server-side only because it called Kubo `pin/ls` directly; v2 cannot, since no endpoint lists an account's pin rows (#826).

## Acceptance

- `plan_prune` cannot be called with a zero keep-count — unrepresentable, not guarded.
- `reclaimed_bytes` equals the sum of the sizes the retire call actually frees, in pinned bytes.
- A pruned 1 GiB version retires across multiple `REGISTRY_BATCH_MAX` batches, leaves before root, and is resumable after a mid-drain restart.
- A retire returning `retired: 0` clears the entry; every other failure retries.
- The pending-reclaim figure drains to zero on hosted confirmation and never on an External-only leg.

## Gate

`Engine Tests`, `Contract Suite`.

---

_Corrected against `main` @ `3d087d673` on 2026-08-06._ Three fixes. (1) The batch cap was cited as `MAX_BATCH = 1000`; that constant lives at `crates/load/src/plan.rs:119` and is an unrelated load-test bound. The real cap is `REGISTRY_BATCH_MAX = 1000` at `crates/engine/src/net/mod.rs:25`, enforced at `crates/engine/src/net/retire.rs:100`. The oldest-first cite `content/retention.rs:78-80` was also stale — that is the `PrunePlan` doc header; the behaviour is at `:82` and `:99-103`.

Closes #849, #850, #851

input.content:
## Problem

The vault settings **write** plane is fully built and reachable from nothing. `publish_settings` (`crates/engine/src/settings.rs:464`) has no production caller — its only references are the re-export at `crates/engine/src/lib.rs:92`, its own `#[cfg(test)]` module, and the `crates/engine/tests/vault_settings.rs` suite. `Command` has seventeen variants and none of them is a settings command.

The **read** half is already wired: `load_settings` is called at `crates/engine/src/facade.rs:1643` inside `Engine::start`, and it already refuses a lapsed record.

The slice that authored the write plane, #870, is closed. No open issue picks the caller up. #643 promises a settings view "over the facade" while no facade command exists, and it is gated behind #635 and #642 in any case.

## Why it matters

A settings record is what carries the account's placement decision. Until a caller exists, no account can ever change its placement away from the cold-start default, and every hardening already landed on this plane — the EOL check from #904, the revision check from #928 — guards a path no user can reach.

It also hides a cliff. `load_settings` is live and fails closed on a lapsed record, so the day a publish caller lands without renewal beside it, the 90-day EOL in #1043 becomes a real availability defect rather than a latent one.

## Scope

- Add the settings command arm to the facade, so a host can write the vault settings record.
- Enrol the published name in the held set in the same change, so `eol_renew_pass` (`crates/engine/src/net/liveness.rs:219`) covers it — this is #1043, which cannot be built before this issue decides the key.
- Thread the command through `crates/wasm/src/host.rs` and `packages/client` so a host can actually call it.

## The held-set key is this issue's decision

`HeldRecords` is `BTreeMap<[u8; 16], HeldRecord>` (`crates/engine/src/net/liveness.rs:91`), keyed by **node id**. The settings record has no node id. Every existing insert comes from `net/resolve.rs:369`, `net/resolve.rs:597`, or `sync/drain.rs:2057`, all of which do have one. So #1043's proposed one-line insert does not type-check as written, and the key is a decision this slice must make, not a detail #1043 can settle on its own.

## Gate

`Engine Tests`. Note that the EOL renewal itself is only reachable under the injected virtual clock — no e2e tier advances wall time, so `crates/engine/tests/vault_settings.rs` is the ceiling for the renewal half.

content.text:
# Resolve PR Review Comments

Resolve all open review comments on the current PR from any automated reviewer (CodeRabbit, GitHub Copilot, etc.) or human reviewers.

## Workflow

### 1. Identify the PR

```bash
PR_NUMBER=$(gh pr view --json number --jq '.number')
```

If no PR exists for the current branch, stop and inform the user.

### 2. Fetch all unresolved review threads

Use the GraphQL `reviewThreads` query to get threads with `isResolved` status:

```bash
REPO_OWNER=$(gh repo view --json owner --jq '.owner.login')
REPO_NAME=$(gh repo view --json name --jq '.name')

gh api graphql -f query="
{
  repository(owner: \"$REPO_OWNER\", name: \"$REPO_NAME\") {
    pullRequest(number: $PR_NUMBER) {
      reviewThreads(first: 100) {
        nodes {
          id
          isResolved
          comments(first: 10) {
            nodes {
              id
              author { login }
              body
              path
              line
              createdAt
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}"
```

Filter to only unresolved threads. If none, report "No unresolved review threads" and stop.

### 3. Triage each comment

For each unresolved thread, read the comment and the referenced code. Categorize as:

- **Valid fix needed** — the comment identifies a real bug, security issue, or meaningful improvement
- **Already addressed** — the issue was fixed in a later commit on this branch
- **Not applicable** — the suggestion doesn't apply (explain why)

### 4. Implement fixes

For all "valid fix needed" comments:

1. Read the referenced file and understand the context
2. Implement the fix
3. Track which thread the fix addresses

Do NOT:

- Make unrelated changes or refactors
- Add features beyond what the comment requests
- Increase timeouts or add retries as a first approach — fix root causes

### 5. Run tests locally

After ALL fixes are implemented:

```bash
# Type check
pnpm typecheck

# Run relevant unit tests
pnpm test

# If E2E-relevant changes were made, run E2E tests too
cd tests/web-e2e && pnpm exec playwright test
```

Do NOT proceed to commit until tests pass. If tests fail, fix the failures first.

### 6. Commit and push

```bash
git add <specific-files>
git commit -m "fix: address PR review comments"
git push
```

### 7. Reply to and resolve each thread

For each thread, reply explaining what was done, then resolve:

- **Fixed comments**: Reply with what was changed and where, then resolve
- **Already addressed**: Reply explaining which commit addressed it, then resolve
- **Not applicable**: Reply with clear reasoning for not making changes, then resolve

Reply via REST (use `--field` not `-f` for `in_reply_to` — must be integer):

```bash
gh api repos/$REPO_OWNER/$REPO_NAME/pulls/$PR_NUMBER/comments \
  --field in_reply_to=COMMENT_ID \
  --raw-field body='...'
```

Resolve via GraphQL (can batch multiple):

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='
mutation {
  resolveReviewThread(input: {threadId: "THREAD_ID"}) {
    thread { isResolved }
  }
}'
```

### 8. Report summary

Print a summary table:

- Thread count resolved
- Fixes made (with file:line references)
- Comments marked as already addressed or not applicable

## Context on what this PR does, so you can triage accurately

- **#1127** — `reseal_scope_root` trusted `entry.recipient_enc_pk` verbatim, so a write-grantee that swapped a victim's `recipientEncPk` under the victim's owner-committed tag redirected every future honest re-seal.

The fix: `WriteWaveNet::remint_grants` (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs`) re-mints every row at the new name via `mint_grant_row`, and `reseal_scope_root` gained `ScopeRootIdentity::owner_enc_secret: Option<&X25519Secret>` — when `Some`, every ledger row must satisfy `recipient_blinded_tag(owner_enc_secret, recipient_enc_pub, identity.ipns_name) == Some(entry.tag)` before anything is sealed. On the write-wave path that check re-validates the re-mint that just happened.

`remint_grants` ordering is deliberate and load-bearing — do not let a reviewer talk you into reordering it:
1. `enforce_committed_ledger` FIRST. Without it, a read grantee that self-upgrades its ledger row to `Write` gets the upgrade minted into the commitment entries, and the owner then signs the escalation and wraps the fresh write scope seed to it.
2. Each row's tag must bind at the **old** name — this is what catches a swapped `recipientEncPk`.
3. Re-mint at the new name.
4. The re-minted `pseudonymPk` must equal the committed one.
5. `expires_at`, `unknown`, and `recipient_identity_pk` carried forward verbatim.

## Already reviewed and deliberately settled — do NOT re-litigate these

An independent crypto review already ran and its findings are folded in. If a reviewer raises one of these, reply with the reasoning and resolve rather than changing code:

- **`recipient_identity_pk` is carried uninterpreted on purpose.** `mint_grant_row` takes it as raw SEC1 bytes. Parsing it would hand a write-grantee a zero-cost veto over the very wave that revokes them, because the field participates in no derivation and nothing else can observe it. There is a test for this: `a_ledger_row_whose_identity_key_is_not_a_curve_point_does_not_stop_the_wave`.

- **The test fixture's fixed `(key, nonce)` reuse is pre-existing on `main` and is test-corpus only.** A plaintext-derived nonce would churn the committed gate KAT vectors and contradict `blueprint/core.md`. Do not "fix" it.

- **The fail-closed-veto surface and the `sweep_pass` leg are filed as #1143.** Out of scope here.

If a reviewer finds a genuinely NEW issue in any of these areas, that is different — fix it and say so.

## Constraints

- Conventional Commits, no parenthesized text in the subject line.
- **Do not push to `main`.** Work on `fix/rotation-grant-tag-remint`.
- The PR is now marked ready — **do not flip it back to draft**, that does not cancel an in-flight review anyway.
- Commit signing can hang on the 1Password agent. Guard with `timeout` if it hangs; **never** pass `--no-gpg-sign`.
- `git fetch` and rebase before pushing.

- If nothing is actionable, say so plainly. Do not manufacture fixes.

## Rebase check before starting this issue

**Recorded 2026-08-07 during wave-7 planning.** PR #1141 changed two shared shapes in the grants layer. This issue does not touch them today, but its scope adds a caller that plausibly will, so check before writing code rather than after.

What changed in #1141:

- `mint_grant_row` now takes `recipient_identity_pk: [u8; IDENTITY_PUBLIC_LEN]` (raw SEC1 bytes), not `&EcdsaVerifier`. Callers pass `verifier.to_sec1()`. The field is carried uninterpreted on purpose — parsing it would hand a write-grantee a veto over the wave that revokes them.
- `ScopeRootIdentity` gained a required `owner_enc_secret: Option<&X25519Secret>` field and now derives `Clone, Copy`. `Some` means the re-seal refuses any ledger row whose `recipientEncPk` does not re-derive the tag it is filed under; `None` skips that check.

Why it may hit this issue: the scope here is `gate::floor::AnchorRole`, `sync/boot.rs`, and a new production shared-scope cold-seed caller for the shared-folder and grant-accept boot paths. #1141 did not touch `gate/floor.rs`, `seams/floor_store.rs`, `sync/boot.rs`, or `grants/accept.rs`, so there is no conflict as the issue stands. The overlap appears only if the new caller lands in `grants/create.rs`, `grants/invite.rs`, or `grants/ledger.rs`, or if it constructs a `ScopeRootIdentity`.

If it does, two rules apply. Pass `Some(owner.enc_secret)` on any leg where the owner provably holds the subkey — #1141 fixed exactly that defect on the parent leg of `create_read_grant`, where a caller-supplied `None` silently disabled the binding check. And keep this issue's own invariant intact: `AnchorRole` is selected from the scope's authenticated position in the vault-index walk, never from a network-supplied field.

`ScopeRootIdentity` construction sites to check against: `grants/create.rs`, `grants/invite.rs`, `net/rotation.rs`, `rotation/cascade.rs`, `rotation/reseal.rs`, `rotation/rotate.rs`, `rotation/sweep.rs`.

**CodeRabbit** posted 1 actionable comment and 2 nitpicks. All three are addressed, and CodeRabbit replied confirming the fix. **Greptile has not reviewed** — 0 threads, 0 reviews. **Macroscope** skipped all five checks, consistent with the exhausted credits.

The actionable finding was real and worth having:

- `owner_root.rs:216` built the grant-blob ephemeral as `[EPH_GRANT_BASE + i as u8; 32]`. `EPH_GRANT_BASE` is `0x60`, so the addition overflows in a debug build at grant index 160, and `i as u8` truncates from 256 — repeating a scalar for the same recipient. The index now widens into the ephemeral tail. Before changing it, the agent confirmed `kat_gen` builds its fixture with `grants: Vec::new()`, so no committed gate KAT vector churns.

The more interesting catch came out of the nitpicks: **every cascade fixture set `owner_enc_secret: None`**, so the propagation this PR added at `cascade.rs:529` was entirely unexercised. There is now a `tag_bound()` builder and a test covering it, and `Owner::committed` mints its ledger tag with `recipient_blinded_tag` at each scope's own name instead of a fake constant. That is the same class of hole that let #1135 survive in the first place — a fixture that never populates the field under test.

It refused both literal suggestions where they were wrong: extending the shared `granted_rows` fixture would have broken `the_re_mint_reproduces_the_committed_pseudonym_key`, which asserts exactly two pseudonym keys.

**CI is green except one leg.** The agent's "still open" list was stale — I checked directly and Engine Tests, Cargo Check & Test (Linux), Contract Suite, Core KATs, Client Browser Suite, FUSE Op Core, Web Bundle, Lint, Tracker Refs, and Web E2E Smoke have all passed. ## Investigated 2026-08-07 against `main` @ `d11bfce11`

Two corrections to how this issue was scoped, plus a trap.

### The blocker is the value shape, not the key

`publish_scope_pointer` (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:1450`) rides `publish_inline`
(`:1456`) — the pointer's `Value` is the sealed block itself, and there is no head CID.
`HeldRecord.head_cid` (`crates/engine/src/net/liveness.rs:63`) is a required `/ipfs/` head, and
`eol_renew_pass` skips any held record whose head is empty (`liveness.rs:245`). So the held set
cannot carry this record as `HeldRecord` stands. That is the whole of this issue's work: an
inline-or-head value shape, plus the enrolment call.

The key is **not** a blocker. `scope_pointer_name(owner_pointer_seed, scope_id)`
(`crates/engine/src/sync/pointer.rs:88`) takes a 16-byte `scope_id`, which fits `HeldRecords`'
`[u8; 16]` key directly.

### This does NOT share a shape change with #1144 and #1043

Earlier wave-7 planning assumed the settings record and the scope pointer needed one common
`HeldRecord` change. They do not — they need complementary halves, and each already has the half
the other lacks. `publish_settings` (`crates/engine/src/settings.rs`) publishes through
`publish_record` with a real head from `preflight_settings`, so its value shape already fits; what
it lacks is a 16-byte id, because `settings_name` derives from the login secret. The pointer is the
mirror image. Neither issue gates the other. Both touch `net/liveness.rs`, so they still should not
run concurrently without coordinating that file.

### Trap: the key space is documented as node ids

`HeldRecords`' own doc (`liveness.rs:91`) says "keyed by node id (`id16`)", and every insert site
passes a `node_id` — `net/resolve.rs:367`, `net/resolve.rs:595`, and `sync/drain.rs:2150`. A
`scope_id` is also 16 opaque bytes, so inserting one into that space breaks the stated invariant,
and a collision with a real node id would **silently evict a live held record** rather than fail.
The liveness loop would then stop renewing whatever it displaced, with no symptom until that record
lapsed at its own EOL.

Either namespace the key so the two spaces provably cannot collide, or state in the type's doc why
they cannot, and cover it with a test. Do not widen the key space silently.

**B8 done — two draft PRs, both `MERGEABLE`.** Every batch now has a PR open: eleven in total.

**[#1146](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/pull/1146) — #1126, the stream-ticket bound.** Bounded by ticket *lifetime* rather than a numeric cap. `MediaBroker.whenIdle` resolves when a ticket's last body ends and reports whether a body ever claimed it, so `downloadSelection`'s sequential loop holds one ticket for a whole selection instead of one per file.

Security review found two real defects there and both are fixed. Settling idle waiters in `MediaBroker.close` was wrong, because a replaced port is the *normal* recovery after a killed Service Worker — the pipe re-opens against the fresh port, so settling revoked the ticket before the retry could name it, and **every cold-worker download would have 404'd**. And the stall deadline could expire on an open body between pulls — a Save-As dialog or a paused download — revoking a live transfer; it now covers only the window before a body claims the ticket.

**[#1160](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/pull/1160) — #1064, the recoverable-refusal surface.** `MediaBroker` reports every read it abandons, classified by `engineErrorCode`; the player shows a retryable notice for a ceiling refusal and a terminal one otherwise, with the media element's own `error` as the floor.

**One deviation from the issue you should know about, and I think the agent was right.** #1064 asks for `cb:media:error` to carry the engine's code across the port. Re-checked against the tree, that would be a dead field: the only `cb:media:error` carrying an engine code is raised by `MediaBroker.fail`, which runs *in the tab* — the same context as the player — and the Service Worker's sole action on it is to error a body whose error a media element cannot read. So `protocol.ts` is untouched and the code is reported tab-side. The reasoning is in the PR body rather than only in this report.

**The two PRs conflict in exactly one file**, and B8 verified it with `git merge-tree` rather than trusting `mergeable=MERGEABLE` — which is the right instinct, since that flag proves nothing about a pairwise merge. Both add a method to the same hand-rolled `MediaService` fake in `FileBrowserActions.test.tsx`. Whichever merges second needs a one-hunk rebase keeping both sides. `broker.ts`, `service.ts` and `service.test.ts` overlap but auto-merge cleanly.

No Puppeteer verification was possible — the player surface needs a logged-in vault, a controlling Service Worker, and the engine at its open-stream ceiling, which the dev server alone cannot reach. Manual steps are in the PR body.

<result>Security review of `feat/fuse-content-write-path` (`git diff main...HEAD`) is complete. No files were edited, nothing committed or pushed.

## 1. Non-zero `ftruncate` resurrects deleted plaintext into the published version

`crates/fuse/src/ops.rs:517-552` — **Severity: MEDIUM**, confidence 9/10. Confirmed.

**Mechanism.** `truncate_handle` records a shrink as only `pending.len = size`. It sets `pending.base = Base::Empty` only when `size == 0` (`ops.rs:547-549`), and `SpillFile::truncate` (`spill.rs:136-149`) only retains/zero-tails blocks the spill *already holds* — on a freshly opened handle the spill is empty, so it is a no-op. `Pending` (`ops.rs:70-79`) carries no truncation floor. Later, `version_block` (`ops.rs:642-652`) resolves any block the spill does not hold by reading the pinned **pre-truncate** base version via `engine.read_stream`, which knows nothing of `pending.len`. `push_version` (`ops.rs:592-598`) then walks `0..len` with no clamp and publishes those bytes.

**Repro — two syscalls, no write needed.** File has a published 100-byte version. `open(O_RDWR)`; `ftruncate(fd, 10)` → `Pending { spill: None, len: 10, base: Version, dirty: true }`; `ftruncate(fd, 100)` → spill is `None` so the spill truncate is a no-op, `len = 100`, `base` stays `Version`; `close(fd)` → every block falls through to the base stream and the published version is byte-for-byte the original 100 bytes. The shrink is entirely undone. The shrink-then-write-past-the-cut variant yields the same for the gap region, which POSIX requires to read as zeros.

**Why security-relevant.** The resurrected plaintext is re-sealed and published as a new *live* version, so (a) a file shared after the user truncated sensitive bytes away exposes those bytes to a recipient who never held the prior version, and (b) the deleted tail is carried into every later version and into a rotated epoch's reseal. Deterministic, no race, reachable from unprivileged `ftruncate(2)`. `create` correctly sets `Base::Empty` (`ops.rs:207`), so this hits exactly the pre-existing-file case where deleted content exists.

**Fix.** Add a truncation floor to `Pending` (e.g. `zeroed_from: Option<u64>`, set on every shrink, raised/cleared as writes fill it). Have `version_block` return zeros — never a base read — for indices wholly at or past the floor, and zero the tail of the straddling block after the base read.

**Test gap.** `crates/fuse/tests/fuse_op_core.rs` exercises truncate only at `size == 0` (lines 986, 1068, 1094, 1115) — the one case `Base::Empty` masks. Add shrink-then-grow and shrink-then-write-past tests.

## 2. `SpillArea::open` sweep + non-atomic dir hardening — UNVALIDATED

`crates/fuse/src/spill.rs:38-46` and `spill.rs:225-229` — candidate severity LOW. **I could not confirm this**: its validation agent never returned, so I have no verdict on it. Correcting an earlier statement of mine in this session that called it filtered — that was premature and wrong.

Raw claim: `open` does `create_dir_all` → `set_permissions(0o700)` → delete **every regular file** in the directory, with no `symlink_metadata` check that the path is a real directory and with a window between creation and the chmod. Claimed consequences: a symlink planted at `<account>/spill` is followed, its target chmod'd `0o700` and its regular files deleted; and the function takes an arbitrary `PathBuf`, so a caller passing `account_data_dir` would wipe the floor store, snapshot cache and staging store. Caveat weighing against it: the attacker must already have same-uid write access to the mount's private data dir, which likely reduces this to hardening. Fix if you want it regardless: reject non-directory/symlink via `symlink_metadata`; create with `DirBuilder::mode(0o700)` so the mode is atomic with creation; scope the sweep to the `spill.<pid>.<n>` name shape.

## Filtered out as false positives

3. **Spill AAD binds no generation counter** (`spill.rs:191`) — FP, confidence 9. Nonce scheme verified **sound**: fresh Entropy-seam key per `SpillFile`, strictly monotone `u64` counter incremented on every `put` including slot rewrites, `checked_add` overflow → `Err`. No nonce is ever reused under a key. Key is `Zeroizing`, memory-only, never logged. The restore-old-ciphertext rollback needs a same-uid local process that can already write the mount directly — hardening, not a vuln.
4. **`release` tears down `Pending` on a failed commit** (`ops.rs:457-465`) — FP, confidence 9. The security hook was factually wrong: `truncated.and(released)` with `release` returning `committed` means the no-handle truncate path returns `Err` on a failed commit, not a false success. `close(2)` is covered by `flush` (`ops.rs:444-446`), which propagates the commit error; the kernel discarding RELEASE's status is the FUSE protocol for every filesystem. Residual (mmap writeback after the last FLUSH) is reliability. Retaining spills after a failed commit would *increase* ciphertext-at-rest lifetime, inverting the PR's goal.
5. **Zero-length write extends the file** (`ops.rs:403-404`) — FP, confidence 8. Mechanically real (`pending.len = pending.len.max(end)` runs unconditionally, so `write(fh, big_offset, &[])` sets the length and marks dirty), but the impact is pure resource exhaustion and the same amplification is reachable via a legitimate one-byte sparse write or `truncate_handle` to any size. Linux VFS short-circuits `count == 0` before FUSE. Worth a one-line `if data.is_empty() { return Ok(0); }` as a correctness fix, not a security finding.

## Verified sound (no finding)

Integer arithmetic on kernel-controlled offsets fails closed throughout (`ops.rs:377` `checked_add`; `ops.rs:647` and `spill.rs:157-163` `checked_mul`). Spill files use `create_new(true)` + `mode(0o600)`, so `O_EXCL|O_CREAT` refuses a planted symlink. Spill truncation and cross-slot transplants fail closed (in-memory `blocks` set, `read_exact` over the full slot, block index in the AAD). `flush`/`fsync` ack only after `stage_op` succeeds and leave `dirty = true` for retry. Write and truncate both refuse non-writable handles (`ops.rs:373-375`, `ops.rs:519-521`). All new plaintext buffers are `Zeroizing`. `spill_io` errors carry only `io::ErrorKind`, never a path or content byte. Entropy is injected via `Box<dyn Entropy>` — no direct `OsRng`/`thread_rng` anywhere in the diff.</result>

## Problem

A partial write over a file whose current version has an **unprojected size** is refused, and there is no path that clears the refusal except waiting for a publish.

`crates/fuse` assembles a new version block by block from three sources: the per-handle spill, the base version, and hole-zeros. To read a block from the base it must know the base version's size. An unprojected size is **unknown, not zero** — guessing zero would silently drop the file's tail into the published version — so the write path fails closed instead.

The engine's read plane resolves **published heads only**. So a file whose `updateContent` is staged in the op queue but not yet published has no resolvable size, and any partial write over it is refused until the publish lands.

## Why it matters

The refusal is correct — failing closed is the only safe choice when the base length is unknown, and #1110's crypto-privacy review already showed what the alternative costs. It found a HIGH defect of exactly this family: a shrink that recorded no floor on the base version re-served bytes a member had truncated away and re-sealed them into the next published version.

But the refusal is user-visible in an ordinary case. Appending to a file that was just written is a normal editor and shell pattern, and the window is however long the op queue takes to drain and publish. The user has no signal that waiting is the remedy.

## Scope

This is an engine-side limitation and cannot be fixed from `crates/fuse`. Two directions, either of which closes it:

- Let the read plane resolve the size of a version that is staged but not yet published, so the base length is known before the publish lands.
- Or carry the staged version's length on the op itself, so a consumer can learn the base length without resolving a head.

Whichever lands, the invariant `crates/fuse` depends on must hold: a base length is either **known** or the write is **refused**. A defaulted or guessed length reintroduces the truncation-resurrection defect.

## Acceptance

- A partial write over a file whose latest `updateContent` is staged but unpublished succeeds, and the published version contains the correct tail.
- No path supplies a defaulted base length. An unknown length still refuses.
- A test covers append-over-staged-version end to end, not only the unit refusal.

## Gate

`Engine Tests`.

`Engine::command` now answers with a `CommandOutcome`, and the `ImportContact` arm answers with the imported `Contact` itself. Nothing in TypeScript can read it.

## Why it matters

`Contact` has no public constructor, so holding one is the proof that its binding verified. Discarding it throws away exactly the evidence the fail-closed import was built to produce. A host that wants to show the user which peer they just added has no way to ask.

This also hides the ordinary case behind a shape that already changed. A later reader sees `command()` returning an outcome and reasonably assumes the import path is live end to end. It is not.

## Scope

- Read the outcome in `packages/client/src/worker/engineHost.ts` instead of discarding it, and carry it back over the worker boundary.
- Surface `identityPublicKey` and `encPublicKey` from the returned value. The WASM boundary hands back an exported class, so the caller must call `.free()` once it has read the fields.
- Keep the queued case working: `CommandOutcome::op_id()` is what the event-correlation path reads, and it must keep flowing.

- A host calling the import command receives the imported contact's two public keys.
- The queued-operation path still correlates by `opId`, with no behaviour change.
- The boundary object is freed after its fields are read, with a test that fails if it leaks.

`Test`, `Typecheck`.

**Wave 7 is fully launched and merge-verified. The result is better than I expected.**

**No branch needs a code fix before it merges.** The cumulative compile check invented zero fixes — every shape change was already absorbed on its own branch. The full eleven-branch merge runs `cargo test --workspace` at 1644 tests passing and `pnpm test` at 837, with wasm32 and `fmt` green.

The three shape-change risks I was worried about all turned out to be non-issues, for checkable reasons: the only FUSE call site discards `command()`'s result, so widening its return type is source-compatible; B1 added the `MalformedInput` arm to the exhaustive `From<EngineError>` impl itself; and nothing outside B4's own branch still referenced the deleted `AnchorRole`.

**File ownership was the right axis.** Across 55 pairs there are two conflicts, both predicted by the batches, both keep-both edits in test files. `write_plane.rs` is about 60 lines of append reassembly — git mis-aligns the shared four-line test preamble as common context and interleaves the hunks — and `FileBrowserActions.test.tsx` is about ten. Each belongs to whichever of its pair merges second.

**Safe merge order:** #1147 → #1151 → #1157 → #1156 → #1149 → #1158 → #1145/#1150/#1146 → #1160. One trap in that list: **#1157 contains #1148**, so never merge #1148 separately afterwards. #1158 owns the `write_plane.rs` resolve and #1160 owns the `.tsx` one.

**One real gap came out of the verification** and is now #1167: the WASM `command()` promise changed from `bigint | undefined` to a `CommandOutcome`, but no TypeScript shipped with it, and it typechecks only because `engineHost.ts:106` discards the result. So the imported contact and its two public keys are unreachable from a host. `Contact` has no public constructor, so discarding it throws away precisely the evidence the fail-closed import exists to produce.

**Three things are yours, not an agent's.** Whether to allow `taiki-e/*` in the Actions allowlist, which closes #1152 and the last cold-cache wall-clock gap. Whether to add `Web Engine WASM` to the required contexts. And #1156 — the FUSE write path handles plaintext at rest, and its `/security-review` was self-performed because the skill agent died twice, so I would put an independent pass on it before it goes ready.

Ten follow-up issues were filed across the wave. Every one arrived orphaned with only `v2-build`; all are now parented, component-labelled, milestoned and edged. I have added that requirement, the no-git-writes rule for review sub-agents, and the cumulative-merge compile check to the shared brief and to memory so the next wave starts from them.

## What

`gate::floor::cold_seed_checked` took the `AnchorRole` as a caller-supplied
argument. The read-epoch (revocation) regression check runs only under
`AnchorRole::Root`, so any caller that could pick `Shared` for the vault anchor
would suppress that check. #774's security and crypto-privacy reviews flagged
this (INFO-1) as the invariant a future shared-scope cold-seed caller must
preserve.

This removes the choice rather than documenting it. The role is now derived
inside `cold_seed_checked` from the re-point's own `scope_id` against the
session's root scope id:

- `session_root_scope_id` is session state derived from the login secret.
- `RepointObject::scope_id` is sealed into the pointer-payload AAD
  (`pointer_ctx(v, object.scope_id)`) and covered by the owner's ECDSA
  signature over the object bytes, so a transport can neither forge it nor
  transplant a shared scope's re-point onto the vault anchor.

Neither operand is network-selectable, and `AnchorRole` is no longer nameable
by any caller — the invariant is structural, not a convention.

Also lands INFO-2: an end-to-end `boot::cold_start` test that seeds the floors
through a first real boot and then trips `ColdStartError::FloorRegression` on a
rolled-back but still validly owner-signed re-point at the same index. The

## The defect

`net::revival::revive` fetched from a single authenticated
`ApiClient::recovery_fetch`, verified the signature, and used the recovered
sequence as the CAS basis. Signature verification proves authorship, not
freshness, so a malicious or compromised recovery endpoint could serve the
user's own older record. The device would then re-mint that superseded head CID
at a fresh, higher sequence and roll itself back to a prior legitimate state —
and, because the sequence is fresh, peers would accept the rollback under the
floor law rather than reject it.

## The fix

Two corroborations before the basis is accepted.

1. **Fan-out corroboration.** `fanout_get_verify` is consulted alongside the
   recovery endpoint; whichever authenticated record has the higher sequence
   becomes the basis. Crucially the head CID is now read from the *same record*
   as the sequence, so a corroborated sequence can never be paired with a stale
   CID — taking `max()` of the sequences alone would have fixed the CAS number
   while still republishing superseded content.

2	# Re-review cycle that holds READY until BOTH CodeRabbit and macroscope land on the

14	  HEAD=$($GH api repos/FSM1/cipher-box/pulls/$PR --jq '.head.sha' 2>/dev/null)
15	  case "$HEAD" in [0-9a-f]*) [ ${#HEAD} -eq 40 ] && break ;; esac
