**Therefore enforcement is necessarily server-side.** I cannot prove the server enforces it from installed client code — flagging that plainly. The strongest available evidence is the vendor's own live-network integration test, `.../session-manager/test/SessionManager.test.ts:166-176`, which asserts `authorizeSession({headers:{origin:'https://malicious-site.com'}})` **rejects**, and `:205-214` that a missing origin header also rejects. **But it is weaker than it looks.** The signature at `sessionManager.js:43` covers `keccak256(encData)` only — `allowedOrigin`, `timeout` and `namespace` travel **outside** the signed payload. **Cost:** the field is public (`mpcCoreKit.js:118,234,1140`), so the only route is replacing `coreKit.sessionManager` with your own `SessionManager` after construction and before `init()`/`createSession`. That is an unsupported reach into SDK internals, not a config line. It is cheaper than #1175 in code volume but relies on undocumented server behaviour plus an unsigned field — I would treat it as a **complement**, not a substitute.

## Q3 — Desync failure behaviour: **two modes, and the bad one wedges the app**

**Mode A — parseable but stale/unredeemable session: graceful.** `«ck»/dist/lib.esm/mpcCoreKit.js:237-239` swallows the `authorizeSession` rejection (`.catch(async err => { log.error(...) })`), and `rehydrateSession`'s own throws (`:1103,:1107`) are caught and only warned at `:1127-1129`. `init()` resolves, `isLoggedIn()` is false, user lands at login, store still usable.

**Mode B — corrupt / undecryptable blob: propagates, then wedges.** `browserStorage.js:43-45` does `JSON.parse((await getItem(...)) || "{}")`; the call at `mpcCoreKit.js:230-232` sits in an `init()` body (`:174-252`) with **no try/catch**. So the throw escapes `restore()`.

Where it lands — `apps/web/src/auth/CoreKitProvider.tsx:66-72`:
```js
const settle = () => { ... if (live) setValue(settled); };
restore.current.then(settle, settle);
```
The **same** `settle` handles fulfil and reject, and `settled` (`:61-65`) is `{session, status:'ready', error:null}`. So a rejected restore is indistinguishable from "restored, signed out": no unhandled rejection, no console surface. `apps/web/src/auth/useAuth.ts:56-57` then computes `isSignedOut === true`, `apps/web/src/routes/FilesPage.tsx:15-17` bounces `/files` to `/`, and `LoginPage.tsx:53,63,74` renders **enabled** login buttons. It fails closed to the front door.

**But it does not self-heal, and it poisons the forward path.** Nothing in `apps/web/src` clears `corekit_store` on a failed restore. A fresh login hits the same `JSON.parse` at `mpcCoreKit.js:1171` (`createSession`) and throws again, surfacing as a raw `SyntaxError` message via `useAuth.ts:67-69` → `LoginPage.tsx:78`. Logout cannot rescue it either: `coreKit.ts:80` is `if (this.isLoggedIn()) await this.coreKit.logout()` and `isLoggedIn()` is false — though #1174's `finally { this.clearStore(); }` at `:81-83` **does** now unconditionally remove the key, so an explicit sign-out click is the escape hatch. A user who never clicks sign-out stays wedged across reloads. There is no `ErrorBoundary` anywhere in `apps/web/src`.

**Why this matters for #1175:** under IDB eviction the wrapping key is *gone* while the blob remains — the expected steady-state failure, not an edge case. An AES-GCM `decrypt` rejection inside `getItem` reproduces Mode B exactly. The wrapper must instead **fail closed by returning `null` and purging the stale blob**, converting the eviction into Mode A. That behaviour is not currently covered by any test: there is no `CoreKitProvider.test.tsx`, the only `restore` overrides in tests are never-settling promises (`apps/web/src/routes/FilesPage.test.tsx:39,:52`), the fake defaults to success (`apps/web/src/test/authFakes.tsx:87`), and `tests/web-e2e/` has zero references to `localStorage` or `corekit_store`.

## Q4 — Multi-tab: **every tab holds a live Core Kit session, unserialised**

**Blueprint** (`/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box/blueprint/web-client.md`): leader election on an exclusive Web Lock `cipherbox-engine` `:88-92`; followers are thin mirrors that spawn no worker and "hold no keys" `:93-95`; failover `:124-127`; Core Kit runs on the UI thread and "login **or session restore** exports the login secret" `:191-196`. The blueprint **never** mentions `corekit_store`, localStorage sealing, or a wrapping key, and never scopes Core Kit to the leader. This is unspecified territory, not unimplemented spec.

**Implementation.** Election `packages/client/src/leadership.ts:59-79`; lock name `packages/client/src/broadcast.ts:138` used at `engineClient.ts:149`; real `navigator.locks` wired at `apps/web/src/engine/createEngineClient.ts:16`.

**Every tab.** `apps/web/src/main.tsx:45` wraps `<App/>` in `<CoreKitProvider createSession={() => createCoreKitSession(...)}>` unconditionally, sibling to `EngineProvider` `:42`. `CoreKitProvider.tsx:24` — "Called once per tab"; `:48-49` `session.current ??= factory.current(); restore.current ??= session.current.restore();` with **no** role or lock condition. content.text:
Recon is in, and it changes the shape of this. Three findings matter more than the rest.

## 1. The issue's threat model overstates what the fix buys

#1175 says the wrapper "converts a silent offline-replayable theft into an attack that has to stay resident in a live tab." That does not hold.

IndexedDB is same-origin readable. A script that reaches the origin opens the database, takes the `CryptoKey` handle, and calls `crypto.subtle.decrypt` — non-extractable blocks export of the *key bytes*, not use of the key. The attacker then exfiltrates the decrypted `sessionId` and replays it offline exactly as today. The wrapper adds one async call to that path.

So the protected class is not "any script that reaches the origin". It is **readers of storage at rest who cannot execute script**: device forensics, a stolen or backed-up browser profile, profile sync, and storage-read-only extension surfaces. That is a real class and worth money, but it is much narrower than the issue claims, and the UX cost lands on every user regardless.

I raised the severity of this yesterday on the offline-replay property. That property is real and unchanged. What I got wrong was treating #1175 as its fix.

## 2. `allowedOrigin` is a dead end, not the cheap win I hoped

It is **not plumbed through mpc-core-kit 3.5.0** — `mpcCoreKit.js:79-82` passes only `sessionTime`, and `allowedOrigin` appears nowhere in the dist. The default resolves to `"*"` (`sessionManager.js:29-33`). Reaching it means replacing `coreKit.sessionManager` after construction, which is an unsupported reach into SDK internals.

And it is weak even then: the signature at `sessionManager.js:43` covers `keccak256(encData)` only, so `allowedOrigin` travels **outside the signed payload**. An attacker holding the stolen `sessionId` holds the scalar and can sign an `updateSession` carrying their own `allowedOrigin: "*"`. Enforcement is server-side and unproven from client code. Not a substitute, and not cheap.

## 3. There is a live wedge bug on `main` today, and it is the real prerequisite

`browserStorage.js:43-45` does `JSON.parse` inside `init()` with no try/catch. A corrupt `corekit_store` throws out of `restore()`. At `CoreKitProvider.tsx:66-72`, `restore.current.then(settle, settle)` passes the **same handler** to fulfil and reject, and `settled` is `{status:'ready', error:null}` — so a failed restore is indistinguishable from "restored, signed out". No unhandled rejection, no console surface.

It fails closed to the front door, which is correct. But nothing clears the store, so the next login hits the same parse at `mpcCoreKit.js:1171` and throws again as a raw `SyntaxError`. The user is wedged across reloads. The only escape is clicking sign-out, because #1174's unconditional `clearStore()` runs in the `finally`.

This matters for #1175 because **IDB eviction reproduces this exact state**: wrapping key gone, blob still present, decrypt rejects inside `getItem`. It is the expected steady state, not an edge case.

## What I recommend

Split it in two, and ship the first half now:

**Step 1 — make a bad store self-healing.** On any restore failure, purge `corekit_store` and land at the front door. Distinguish reject from resolve in `CoreKitProvider`. This is small, it fixes a real user-facing defect that exists today independent of #1175, and without it #1175 converts an eviction into a permanent wedge. There is no `CoreKitProvider.test.tsx` at all, so it needs one.

**Step 2 — the wrapper**, on top of that, with its value restated honestly as at-rest protection.

The implementation cost of step 2 is larger than the issue suggests. `clearStore` at `coreKit.ts:91-93` is synchronous and the field is typed `Storage`, so both change. Five #1174 tests assert store identity or read plaintext back synchronously (`coreKit.test.ts:63,79,89,100,112`) and need rewriting — the gate we just landed is the thing that breaks. Every tab runs `CoreKitProvider` with no lock (`main.tsx:45`, `CoreKitProvider.tsx:48-49`), and nothing serialises across tabs, so concurrent cold starts race the wrapping-key get-or-create; the loser's ciphertext becomes permanently undecryptable. The `LockManagerLike` seam at `leadership.ts:22-29` already exists for this.

v1 has the primitive twice (`v1:apps/web/src/lib/device/identity.ts:50-68`, `search-index.service.ts:333-346`), but it does not transfer: both derive the key by HKDF from the vault private key, which only exists *after* login. #1175 must open *before* login, so it has to persist the `CryptoKey` object itself — a structurally weaker construction. v1's `STORAGE_VERSION` migration is worth copying.

## The decision I need from you

1. **Split as above** — ship the self-heal fix this wave, plan the wrapper properly. My recommendation.
2. **Both together as one PR** — one review cycle, but a bigger diff on auth code and the test rewrite tangles with the bug fix.
3. **Re-scope #1175 first** — rewrite the issue body to the corrected threat model and decide afterwards whether the at-rest class justifies the persistence cost.

One more thing worth knowing before you choose: `@toruslabs/customauth` writes its own `torus_login_*` keys straight to `window.localStorage` during the OAuth redirect (`StorageHelper.js:47,52,76,82`). Those sit outside the `storage` option entirely, so #1175 does not seal them.

#1173 flips at 12:44:59Z as planned.

Im fully behind step 1, but still very skeptical about the ux tradeoff made in step 2. Additionally, if I am reading this all correctly, step 2 can safely be implemented later on should I decide that the actual security gap is wide enough to warrant the complexity.
Your reading is correct, with one date attached to it. Let me confirm the facts rather than assert them.

**Nothing depends on #1175** — no dependents in the native dependency graph, zero cross-references. It is a leaf. Deferring it moves nothing else.

**Step 1 makes step 2 easier, not harder.** The self-heal path is precisely the failure mode the wrapper needs (decrypt rejects → purge → front door). Building it now means step 2 later is the wrapper plus the test rewrite, with its hardest failure case already solved and covered.

**There is no format lock-in.** The SDK writes a single JSON blob under one key, `corekit_store` (`mpcCoreKit.js:38`). Introducing a wrapper later makes existing plaintext blobs fail to open, and step 1's purge then signs those users in again. That is a one-time re-login on staging, not a migration and not data loss — the login secret comes from Web3Auth, never from local storage. So even past the #653 cutover the deferral cost stays mild.

Your skepticism on the UX trade is well placed, and the corrected threat model is what makes it defensible to wait: the residual exposure while step 2 sits unbuilt is at-rest reads by an attacker who cannot run script, against an 8-hour window. A script attacker is unaffected by step 2 either way.

I filed step 1 and put the edge in.

## Goal

Stop the Core Kit store from holding a bearer capability that a reader of storage at rest can take
off the device.

## Threat model — corrected 2026-08-08

An earlier revision of this issue claimed the wrapper "converts a silent offline-replayable theft
into an attack that has to stay resident in a live tab". **That is wrong**, and the correction is
what moved this issue to low priority.

IndexedDB is same-origin readable. A script that reaches the origin opens the database, takes the
`CryptoKey` handle and calls `crypto.subtle.decrypt`. `extractable: false` blocks export of the key
bytes, not use of the key. The attacker reads the plaintext `sessionId` and replays it offline
exactly as before. The wrapper adds one async call to that path and nothing else.

So the class this protects is **readers of storage at rest who cannot execute script in the
origin**: device forensics, a stolen or synced browser profile, a backup, and storage-read-only
extension surfaces. That class is real, but it is far narrower than "any script on the origin", and
the cost falls on every user.

What remains true, and is the reason this issue exists at all: `corekit_store.sessionId` is a
secp256k1 scalar that both addresses and decrypts a Web3Auth-held record carrying `postBoxKey`,
`factorKey`, `tssShare` and `signatures`. What that exports is the login secret, the root of the key
hierarchy in `blueprint/core.md`. Rotation cannot help, because the holder has the root rather than
a scope.

`allowedOrigin` is not an alternative. It is not plumbed through mpc-core-kit 3.5.0 — the session
manager is built with `sessionTime` alone (`mpcCoreKit.js:79-82`) and the default resolves to `"*"`
(`sessionManager.js:29-33`). Reaching it means replacing `coreKit.sessionManager` after
construction, and the field travels **outside** the signed payload (`sessionManager.js:43`), so a
holder of the stolen `sessionId` can sign an `updateSession` carrying their own value.

## Current controls

- `SESSION_SECONDS` caps the window at 8h (`apps/web/src/auth/coreKit.ts:107`, landed by #913).
- `clearStore()` tears the store down on logout and on the failed-login rollback
  (`apps/web/src/auth/coreKit.ts:91-93`, landed by #913).

## Work

Hand Core Kit an `IAsyncStorage` wrapper rather than `window.localStorage` directly. `AsyncStorage`
awaits every store read and write (`browserStorage.js:21-57`; all six SDK call sites confirmed
awaited), so an AES-GCM wrapper drops in on the SDK side.

- Generate the wrapping key with `extractable: false` and keep it in IndexedDB.
- Keep the store origin-wide — the failover re-export still needs it (#913).
- Clear the wrapping key on logout, alongside the store teardown #913 added.

Known implementation cost, established 2026-08-08:

- `clearStore()` is synchronous and the field is typed `Storage` (`coreKit.ts:37,91-93`). Both
  change; `IAsyncStorage` has no `removeItem` and no sync surface.
- Five tests landed by #913 assert store identity or read the plaintext back synchronously
  (`coreKit.test.ts:63,79,89,100,112`). The gate #913 landed is the thing this breaks.
- Every tab runs `CoreKitProvider` with no lock (`main.tsx:45`, `CoreKitProvider.tsx:48-49`) and
  nothing serialises across tabs, so concurrent cold starts race the wrapping-key get-or-create and
  the loser's ciphertext becomes permanently undecryptable. The `LockManagerLike` seam at
  `packages/client/src/leadership.ts:22-29` exists for this.
- The web-e2e allow-list inspects `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` only
  (`tests/web-e2e/tests/smoke.spec.ts:87-93`). A wrapping-key database would pass unseen.
- `@toruslabs/customauth` writes its own `torus_login_*` keys straight to `window.localStorage`
  during the OAuth redirect (`StorageHelper.js:47,52,76,82`). Those sit outside the `storage`
  option, so this issue does not seal them.

v1 has the primitive twice — `v1:apps/web/src/lib/device/identity.ts:50-68` and
`v1:apps/web/src/services/search-index.service.ts:333-346` — but neither transfers. Both derive the
key by HKDF from the vault private key, which exists only after login, and this wrapper must open
before login. v1's `STORAGE_VERSION` migration is still worth copying.

## Gate

web unit, over the wrapper: a round trip through it, and a stored value that is not the plaintext.
Extend the web-e2e allow-list to enumerate `indexedDB.databases()`.

## When to reconsider

Pull this forward if any of these becomes true:

- The at-rest class stops being acceptable — for example a decision to support shared or managed
  devices, or a compliance requirement covering data at rest in the browser profile.
- Web3Auth plumbs `allowedOrigin` through mpc-core-kit and pins it server-side at first set, which
  would change the residual exposure independently of this work.
- The session window stops being capped at 8h.

## Deferral safety

Nothing depends on this issue. The SDK writes a single JSON blob under one key `corekit_store`
(`mpcCoreKit.js:38`), so there is no format to lock in. Introducing the wrapper later makes existing
plaintext blobs fail to open, and the purge from #1182 signs those users in again — a one-time
re-login, not a migration and not data loss, since the login secret comes from Web3Auth rather than
from local storage.

## Dependencies

Sequenced behind #913, which landed the storage decision and the logout teardown this builds on, and
behind #1182, which makes an unreadable store self-healing. Without #1182 an evicted wrapping key
turns an ordinary IndexedDB eviction into a permanent wedge.

#1175 is marked down. `priority:low`, applied and verified.

I created the label rather than reused one — no priority scheme existed in this repo, so I followed the established `comp:` / `wayfinder:` namespace. Its description carries the rule so it means something on sight: *"Deferred by decision — do not pull into a wave unless the recorded condition changes."*

But a label alone would not have done what you asked. The body was the actual hazard: its Problem section claimed "any script that reaches the origin reads 32 bytes and replays them offline", which is the framing that got it escalated in the first place. A planner reading that in three weeks pulls it forward again regardless of a label. So I rewrote it:

- **A deferral banner at the top**, dated, pointing at the condition.
- **The corrected threat model**, stated as a correction with the reasoning — that `extractable: false` blocks export of the key bytes, not use of the key, so the protected class is at-rest readers who cannot execute script.
- **Why `allowedOrigin` is not an alternative**, so nobody re-derives that dead end.
- **A "When to reconsider" section** giving three concrete triggers: the at-rest class stops being acceptable (shared or managed devices, a compliance requirement), Web3Auth plumbs `allowedOrigin` through and pins it server-side, or the 8h cap goes away.
- **A "Deferral safety" section** recording why waiting is cheap — no dependents, a single JSON blob so no format lock-in, and a one-time re-login as the worst case.
- **The implementation cost** from the recon, so a future planner sizes it correctly instead of from the optimistic original.

I also kept what remains true and load-bearing: the `sessionId` still exports the login secret, and rotation cannot help against a root compromise. Marking it low priority is a judgement about the width of the gap, not a claim the gap is gone.

One thing I did **not** do, because it is your call and it changes what ships: **#1175 is still on the v2.0.0 milestone.** If wave scoping draws from that milestone, it will keep appearing there even at low priority. Dropping it from v2.0.0 is the stronger signal and says it does not ship in v2. Want me to remove it, or leave it in-milestone and let the label carry the weight?

## The gap

`accept_share` is generic over `S: ReceivedShareStore` (`crates/engine/src/grants/accept.rs:396`) and must durably persist before it acks: a sequence floor that advanced ahead of a failed persist strands the share below it forever, so persist-fail returns un-acked and the item redelivers (`crates/engine/src/grants/accept.rs:240-247`).

`ReceivedShareStore` (`crates/engine/src/grants/accept.rs:248`) has exactly one implementor — `InMemoryReceivedShareStore` (`crates/engine/src/testkit/fakes/received_share_store.rs:38`). `testkit` is behind the `test-kit` feature, and `crates/engine/Cargo.toml:14-15` states production builds never compile it. There is therefore no store a production `accept_share` call can be handed, and no production call site exists.

## Why this is a decision, not one more impl

The trait's own doc calls it "a grants-layer seam, not one of the nine host seams", whose concrete store the facade wires "when the accept flow is mounted" (`crates/engine/src/grants/accept.rs:245-247`). But `SeamSet` (`crates/engine/src/seams/mod.rs:112`) makes field-struct construction the compile-time completeness gate — no optional seams, no defaults (`crates/engine/src/seams/mod.rs:108-111`). Adding a tenth seam is a breaking change to `SeamTypes` (`crates/engine/src/seams/mod.rs:85`) and to every implementor: `WebSeamTypes` (`crates/wasm/src/host.rs:45`, constructed at `:114`) and `FakeSeamTypes` (`crates/engine/src/testkit/world.rs:14`, constructed at `:110`), plus the desktop seam set when it lands.

Settle one of the two shapes and land it:

- a tenth host seam, with its conformance kit and every host's implementation, or
- a grants-layer store the facade builds over an existing durable seam, leaving `SeamSet` at nine

Whichever wins, `crates/engine/src/grants/accept.rs:245-247` must stop describing a store that does not exist.

## Checkable condition

- an `accept_share` call site exists outside any `#[cfg(test)]` module and outside the `test-kit` feature
- an accepted share survives a process restart, and a redelivered mailbox item re-accepts idempotently against the persisted list
- a persist failure leaves the item un-acked with the sequence floor untouched, and the redelivery self-heals the bookmark

The user is happy to batch **multiple loosely-related issues into one PR** to keep review cadence
flowing. Stated 2026-08-08 during wave 8.

**Why:** CodeRabbit gives one review per hour org-wide, so a wave of N single-issue PRs costs at
least N hours of review chain whatever order it runs in. The file-ownership graph caps how much can
run in *parallel*; the review slot caps how fast anything *lands*. Batching cuts the number of
cycles, and it is the only lever that moves the real bottleneck. See
[[project-v2-hot-file-contention-caps-parallelism]] for the other half of the constraint.

**How to apply:**

- Batch by **shared file surface first, topical relation second**. Two issues that both touch
  `facade.rs` belong together whether or not they are conceptually related, because splitting them
  guarantees a rebase. Two issues in the same subsystem that interact semantically (one changes
  where auth state comes from, the other what happens when restore fails) belong together because
  splitting them makes the second rework the first.
- 2–3 issues per PR is the working size. Do not build one giant PR: review quality drops, and
  CodeRabbit has a [[project-coderabbit-150-file-cap]].
- Give each issue its own commit inside the batch, and a `Closes #N` line per issue in the body.
- When adding scope to an agent already mid-build, tell it to finish the original issue coherently
  first and add the second on top — and to ship the first alone if the second turns out much larger
  than scoped. A blocked bug fix is worse than an extra review cycle.
- Still hold a batch behind a genuine blocker. Batching changes how work is grouped, never whether
  a dependency edge is respected.

Related: [[feedback-closes-vs-part-of-issue-hygiene]] (one `Closes` per finished issue),
[[feedback-keep-prs-draft-control-cr-timing.md]] (the orchestrator owns slot timing).

**1. `net/retire.rs:189` — CRITICAL, subset-coverage replacement. ACCEPTED, real, data loss.**
Held `{L1}` + incoming `{L2}` → stored `{L2}`, and `L1` was then retired while a retained version still named it. Confirmed against the crate's own ranking (`orphaned_head`: unpinning a live-named block is loss, a stale row is only a leak).

The key thing CodeRabbit's suggestion missed: a union **cannot be re-derived at the ledger**. `owed_bytes = manifest − w(retained)`, and the ledger has no per-CID weights, so it cannot compute `w(A ∪ B)`. Storing the union while keeping either figure would have made `retire_owed`'s `retirable.pinned_bytes != entry.owed_bytes` gate fail forever — trading the loss for a permanently undrainable debt. So three changes landed together: union of retained; `owed_bytes = min(held, incoming)` redocumented as a **ceiling**; gate relaxed `!=` → `>`.

That ceiling is loose by exactly the shared weight on a merged entry, and my security pass found a working data-loss exploit through the slack (bend one retained CID in the store → recomputed figure reproduces the ceiling exactly → gate passes → the displaced leaf is retired). I reproduced it, then closed it by requiring `entry.retained ⊆ expansion.cids()` — an invariant honest entries hold by construction. Conformance kit moved to the union rule with the disjoint case, so the kit can't enforce the bug.

**2. `sync/drain.rs:1736` — MAJOR, debt lost if `owe` fails after publish. MECHANISM CONFIRMED, fix deferred to a filed issue (#1184).**
Verified end to end: `publish_node` → `mark_published` on the record ack → `queued_ops` drops any op at/below the mark → replay reloads the *published* short history so `plan_prune` finds nothing. Result is a leak, on the correct side of the crate's ranking. Both orderings reachable without a new protocol are worse or equal (`owe` before publish = loss on a failed publish; `owe` before `mark_published` = no improvement). A real fix needs a pre-journalled intent **plus** a reconciliation sweep carrying the originating node — neither exists, and an intent without reconciliation is a staging leak stacked on the pin leak. Filed as **issue #1184** with the full trace.

**3. `sync/drain.rs:1793` — MINOR, aliasing between doomed versions. ACCEPTED, but the sketch was NOT applied literally — it introduces a permanent leak.**
`protected.extend(retirable.cids())` includes the entry's own root. A history may name one `contentCid` twice (the upstream guard only refuses doomed-vs-survivor overlap), so the repeat's whole expansion lands in `protected` → `owed_bytes: 0`, retained containing its own root → merged entry protects its expansion key → `root != entry.target` defers it forever. I reproduced that. `prune_debt` now *also* skips an already-charged root.

The finding, `net/rotation.rs:1415`: the write-floor check is not atomic with root publication. The floor can rise between `write_epoch_floor` returning at :1412 and `publish_record` completing. Another device advances the floor to `node.write_epoch` or higher while this wave publishes the parked root, and if that root becomes canonical its write body sits at or below the durable floor and can never reopen.

It is also structurally the same shape as the Major on #1173: a check that is correct in isolation but not durable against a concurrent writer. Delegating it.

=== #1179 ===
engine: the write wave carries a writer-authored writeHistoryLink into the owner-signed moved root [OPEN]
## Problem

`WriteWaveNet::reseal_root` carries `plane.write_body.write_history_link` verbatim into the moved root's re-sealed write body (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs`, the `CommittedSet` it hands `reseal_scope_root`).

`WriteBody` is sealed under `writeScopeSeed`, which **every** write grantee holds — including the one the rotation is cutting. `write_history_link` is opaque bytes (`crates/core/src/seal/write_body.rs`), no owner signature covers it, `enforce_committed_ledger` does not reach it, and `reseal_scope_root` copies it unexamined.

## Why it matters

Two compounding problems:

1. **Semantic wrong-seed.** The wave mints a *fresh* `writeScopeSeed` but republishes the *pre-rotation* write history link, so the moved root's link does not chain to the seed it was just re-keyed to.
2. **Capability widening once seed recovery lands.** `RotateScopeWritePlan::resume_write_scope_seed` is documented as "the fresh write scope seed recovered from the published root (the write-plane history link)" (`crates/engine/src/rotation/rotate_write.rs`), and that recovery wiring is not landed. When it lands, a revoked write grantee who plants a forged `writeHistoryLink` before the wave gets the **owner to sign it into the new root**, and the resumed wave then republishes the whole subtree under names derived from an attacker-chosen seed. Total write-plane takeover, in a record that is owner-authentic — no gate stage can catch it.

The only thing keeping this latent is that the recovery is unbuilt.

## Resolving

The wave must mint its own link rather than carry one: either pass an empty `write_history_link` from `reseal_root` (the wave holds its own seed; recovery is not this record's job), or extend `ResealSeeds` with a write-plane `prev` and have `reseal_scope_root` seal a fresh link over the retiring `writeScopeSeed` under `write_key(fresh_seed)`, mirroring the read-plane `prev` path.

Independently, when the seed recovery lands it must cross-check `derive_write_name(recovered_seed, scope_id) == published root name` before a single republish — the reverse of the check `publish_moved` already makes in the forward direction.

## Gate

Engine unit:

- a planted `writeHistoryLink` on the pre-wave root is never re-signed into the moved root
- a resumed wave refuses a recovered write scope seed that does not derive the published root name

## Notes

Found by the `/security-review` gate on #1177. Pre-existing; the fix lands in `crates/engine/src/rotation/reseal.rs` and `rotate_write.rs`, owned by other slices.

Part of #655

=== #1139 ===
engine: a resumed write rotation cannot recover its write scope seed, because nothing mints the write-plane history link [OPEN]
## Problem

Nothing in the repo ever mints a `WriteBody.write_history_link`. `reseal_scope_root` copies whatever it is handed (`crates/engine/src/rotation/reseal.rs:467`), and every call site passes `&[]` or passes the old value through — including `WriteWaveNet::reseal_root` (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:1232`).

A `Slot::Unreadable` contributes `None`. That is not an oversight that can be
patched at this layer — the revision lives *inside* the sealed, det-CBOR body
(`StoredList::encode` writes `"revision"` into the map at
`crates/engine/src/grants/accept.rs`), so a slot whose seal will not open, or
whose body carries a `v` this build refuses
(`ReceivedSharesCodecError::UnsupportedVersion`), has a revision that is
genuinely unknowable here.

Consequence: when one slot is unreadable and the other is free, a persist writes
revision `1` beside bytes that may hold a much higher revision. A build that
*can* read both then loads the higher revision — the older list — and the
accepted shares the downgraded session bookmarked are lost. `load` picks the
higher revision at `received_share_store.rs:185`, so the inversion is silent.

## Why it is live now

Before the slot-selection fix this state could not persist: the old target
selection overwrote the unreadable slot in the `(Unreadable, Empty)` orientation,
destroying the forward list outright. That was the worse failure — unrecoverable
loss of a whole list — and preserving the unreadable slot is the right trade. But
the trade is what makes a revision inversion reachable, so it should be recorded
rather than left implicit.

Reachability is currently narrow: it needs a build that writes a `v` this build
rejects, and v2 is pre-release with no deployed older builds. It is a
forward-compatibility debt, not a present-day defect.

## Why it matters beyond this store

The two-slot-with-monotonic-revision layout here is the reference pattern for the
contact store and the invite store, because `StagingStore::put_staged_bytes`
promises no atomic replace. Both inherit this gap verbatim.

## Options

1. **Accept and document.** Treat a downgraded session's lost increments as the
   expected cost of running an old build. Cheapest; leaves the silent inversion.
2. **Put the revision where a refusing reader can still see it.** A fixed-position
   header ahead of the version-sensitive body, or an authenticated-but-clear
   field, would let `newest` account for a slot it cannot fully decode. This is a
   `crates/core` wire change: new KAT vectors, idempotent regeneration, and the
   encode/decode fail-closed symmetry rule (AGENTS.md rule 8) all apply.
3. **Refuse a persist whose monotonicity cannot be established.** Rejected on
   inspection: a single torn first write leaves `(Unreadable, Empty)`, so this
   would brick the store permanently on a very ordinary failure.

Option 2 is the only one that actually closes it, and it should be decided
*before* the contact and invite stores copy the layout, not after.

## Acceptance

- A decision recorded on options 1–3, and if 2, the header shape frozen in
  `crates/core` with KAT vectors.
- A test pinning that a persist beside an unreadable slot cannot produce a
  revision a later reader ranks below the bytes it preserved.
- Whatever is decided is stated once at the definition, so the contact and invite
  stores inherit it rather than rediscover it.

A single slot that refuses and surfaces an error fails closed instead.

**Option 3 is already dead** — refusing a persist whose monotonicity is unknown bricks the store on a single torn first write, which leaves `(Unreadable, Empty)`.

It also killed the argument I would have made for keeping it: two slots never protected concurrent writers either. Two writers both read revision N and write N+1 into different slots, and one list is lost just as with one key. Safety comes from tab leadership, not the layout.

**Migration is one file.** `StoredList.revision` lives in the engine codec, not core, so the KAT vectors are untouched. Roughly 100 lines deleted from `received_share_store.rs`, keeping `revision` as a monotonic write counter.

## What I propose

Batch A becomes **#1164 + #1165 + the collapse**, as one PR, after #1194 merges. All three are grants-layer stores, the collapse is a deletion in the same directory, and it lands as "three stores, one key each" rather than two new stores copying a pattern being deleted beside them. That also gives #1189 a code change to close against rather than closing it as an argument.

Batch A therefore now waits on **#1194 merging** rather than on the #1189 decision — a cleaner gate, and one you control.

One thing I would like to file: **the kit is opt-in.** A host that calls `check` and skips `check_failed_put` is silently only half-held. Batch A is **#1164 + #1165 + collapsing the two-slot layout**, as one PR, after #1194 merges.

`StagingReceivedShareStore` was built with two slots and a monotonic revision **only** because
`put_staged_bytes` promised no failure-atomic replace. #1194 fixes that at the seam, which makes the

So **#1164 and #1165 write a single key each**, not two slots. Their issue bodies carry a
"Shape — decided" section pointing at the `RetireLedger` precedent (`crates/engine/src/seams/mod.rs:5-10`)
— that half is still right, `SeamSet` stays at nine — but the two-slot half is now wrong. Fix those
bodies before launching, or the agents will build the pattern being deleted beside them.

- **#1187 + #1188.** The write-epoch floor guard is not atomic with the root publish. Unreachable

- **#1192, #1193, #1191** are all edged as blockers of **#764**. A #764 plan must read all three.

Two, because I started two background commands. Each one gets a zsh wrapper from the Bash tool plus the script it runs — my earlier `awk '{print $NF}'` printed only the last argument, which made five processes look like unrelated fragments.

```
29128  Claude Code
├─ 19823  zsh wrapper
│  └─ 19825  chain-wave8d.sh 1786207767        the review queue: #1194 → #1190 → #1183
│     └─ 19827  recycle-keepready.sh 1194      the current cycle, waiting out the slot
└─ 19843  zsh wrapper
   └─ 19845  verdict-watch2.sh …1194.log       fires on #1194's verdict
```

So it is two logical jobs, not two strays.

**Why both exist:** the chain notifies me only when it *finishes* — all three PRs, roughly three hours out. That is how #1174's verdict sat unnoticed in a log earlier until you told me it had landed. The watcher closes that gap by exiting the moment a verdict appears, which forces a notification per PR. They are complementary rather than duplicated: the chain does the work, the watcher wakes me.

`recycle-keepready.sh` (19827) is a child of the chain, not a separate job — it is the cycle currently running for #1194, sleeping out the 2,638 seconds to its slot.

The one that genuinely was a stray is already gone: the watcher I orphaned by reordering the queue, pointing at a log I had deleted. That is the tear-down rule worth keeping — killing a chain means killing its watcher in the same breath, since a watcher whose subject vanishes waits forever without complaining.

`Command::Grant` (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:465`), `Command::Revoke` (`:474`) and `Command::Downgrade` (`:482`) each name the recipient by `recipient_identity_public_key` alone.

The grant path needs more. `GrantRecipient` (`crates/engine/src/grants/create.rs:91`) carries `enc_pub` (`:100`) — the X25519 key the grant blob and the sealed share pointer are HPKE-sealed to — and `create_read_grant` (`crates/engine/src/grants/create.rs:261`) mints the row from it at `:312`. The blinded tag is `ECDH(ownerEnc, recipientEnc) ‖ scopeRootIpnsName` (`blueprint/core.md:277`), so an identity key alone cannot even derive the tag.

`import_contact` (`crates/engine/src/grants/contact.rs:49`) is the only way to obtain that bound pair, and the engine drops the `Contact` it returns. Nothing in the tree stores one — there is no contact store of any kind, and `SeamSet`'s nine fields (`crates/engine/src/seams/mod.rs:112`) have no durable home for owner-local contact state.

`Contact` has no public constructor precisely so that holding one is proof the binding signature verified (`crates/engine/src/grants/contact.rs:19-25`). A grant path that pairs an `identity_pk` from one source with an `enc_pub` from another seals the read scope seed to an attacker-chosen X25519 key while routing the share pointer to the honest recipient's inbox, who cannot open it — the silent key-substitution attack #962 describes. There is no directory to re-fetch a subkey from; the contact code is the only channel.

## Checkable condition

- an imported `Contact` survives a session restart, and a later `Grant` naming only that recipient's identity key reaches `create_read_grant` carrying the subkey that import verified
- a `Grant` naming an identity key that was never imported fails closed with a typed error, and no code path constructs a recipient from an unverified subkey
- the lookup key is the same identity key the grant ledger entry and the mailbox address use, so `Revoke` and `Downgrade` resolve the recipient the grant was minted for
- nothing persists an unverified pair — the store's only writer is the fail-closed import

#962 makes `GrantRecipient` carry the bound pair as one value so the verified import is the only way in. That is the type change; this issue is the storage that gives the facade a `Contact` to hand it. They land together at the first production `GrantRecipient` caller.

leave `SeamSet` at nine.

`RetireLedger` is "the exception that proves the shape — the same trait contract, with a conformance
kit of its own, but the engine ships the implementation over a seam every host already provides."

it already provides.

Follow #1185 for the concrete pattern: a grants-layer store type, a conformance kit on the
`RetireLedger` precedent, and durable state carried where the op queue, op marks and retire ledger
already live.

## Commit 1 — collapse the two-slot layout

`crates/engine/src/grants/received_share_store.rs` (515 lines) stores its list across two slots with a monotonic `revision`, chosen only because `StagingStore::put_staged_bytes` promised no failure-atomic replace. PR #1194 landed that atomicity at the seam (merged as `550192b9b`), so the layout is now redundant — and worse than redundant. When one slot is unreadable it is usually the *newer* one, so the `[Slot::Held(held), _] | [_, Slot::Held(held)]` arm at `:190` serves the older list and silently drops what the newer session bookmarked. A single key returns the "stored list did not open" error instead, which is the fail-closed behaviour the design prefers everywhere else.

Collapse it to one staging key. `slot_keys()` (`:67`), `read_slots` (`:93`), `Slot` (`:103`), `Slot::revision` (`:115`), `TargetPreference` (`:122`-`:146`) and `StoredList.revision` all go. `StoredList.revision` lives in the **engine** codec, not `crates/core`, so no KAT vectors move — confirm that yourself before you rely on it.

Several encode real invariants that survive the collapse (`a_lost_write_never_destroys_the_readable_list` `:352`, `an_entropy_failure_leaves_the_stored_list_untouched` `:499`, `a_list_this_session_cannot_open_fails_closed_rather_than_reading_empty` `:282`, `orphan_gc_never_collects_the_persisted_list` `:333`). The slot-arbitration tests (`:380`, `:401`, `:425`, `:456`, `:486`) become meaningless — say which you removed and why in your report. Add a test proving an unreadable single key fails closed rather than reading as empty.

This also resolves issue #1189 (the stale-slot inversion). Put `Closes #1189` in the PR body.

Commit 2: the contact store for #1164. Commit 3: the invite-record store for #1165. Build each on the pattern `received_share_store.rs` shows **after** your collapse — a grants-layer store type plus a conformance kit on the `RetireLedger` precedent. Read `crates/engine/src/net/retire.rs:139` (`StagingRetireLedger`) too.

- #1164: a `Grant` naming an identity key that was never imported must fail closed with a typed error, and **no code path may construct a recipient from an unverified subkey**. `Contact` has no public constructor precisely so holding one proves the binding signature verified (`crates/engine/src/grants/contact.rs:19-25`). Pairing an `identity_pk` from one source with an `enc_pub` from another is the silent key-substitution attack. The store's only writer must be the fail-closed import.
- #1165: `RecordedInvite.expires_at` is the authority; the published `expiresAt` is a cooperating-reader hint any write-grantee can strip or forge (`crates/engine/src/grants/invite.rs:242-262`). Also: a mint whose record fails to persist must not return a usable URL fragment to the host — an unclaimable link is worse than a refused mint.

**29 worktrees removed, 4 kept.** Main is clean at `550192b9b`.

Kept, and why:

| Worktree | Reason |
|---|---|
| `wt-batchA` | live agent, now at `813cc466f` — it is committing |
| `wt-batchB` | #1190, in the review slot right now |
| `wt-1182` | #1183, queued for the next slot |
| `agent-a68078a748ffa8953` | 34 staged changes — see below |

The thing worth your attention is that last one. **Ancestry said all 33 worktrees were stale**, including the branch for #1194 that I had just watched merge. The repo squash-merges, so a merged branch is never an ancestor of `main` and `merge-base --is-ancestor` reports every one of them unmerged. I switched to PR state from GitHub, which sorted them properly: 21 merged, 3 closed, 5 review scratch with no PR, 3 in flight. Had I trusted ancestry and inverted it into "keep what looks unmerged", I would have kept everything and cleaned nothing.

Worktree removal cannot lose commits — the branch ref keeps them, so any of these is recoverable with `git worktree add`. The one exception is uncommitted working-tree state, which is why the dirty one stayed.

**`agent-a68078a748ffa8953` holds 34 staged changes on `feat/prune-retire-ledger`, whose PR #1158 is already merged.** All 34 are staged rather than working-tree edits, they span `.github/`, `blueprint/`, `crates/engine`, `crates/fuse` and `crates/wasm` with no common theme, and three are deletions of files that exist at its HEAD. A second worktree held the same branch clean. That reads as a stale index from a reset, not authored work — but "reads as" is not "is", and it is the one case where deleting would destroy something. It costs nothing to leave until you say otherwise.

`cumwt` was a detached merge simulation of `fix/rotation-repoint-channels`, which merged as #1177; I removed it since the question it answered is settled.

content.text:
**Docker is back and the CipherBox stack is fully healthy** — all five containers up and passing health checks, no manual start needed.

What happened: graceful quit failed, because the wedge blocked Docker's own shutdown path. I escalated to SIGTERM, then SIGKILL for the two that survived. Only `com.docker.vmnetd` remained, which is correct — it is the root-owned privileged helper launchd keeps alive by design. The daemon came back in about 10 seconds on server 29.5.2.

**The restart cleared the symptom, not the cause.** Your Mac was never short of space — 81 GiB free. What filled was Docker's own VM disk, and it is still nearly as full as when it wedged:

| | total | reclaimable |
|---|---|---|
| Build cache | 12.34 GB | **9.33 GB** |
| Images | 15.31 GB | 11.59 GB (75%, 9 dangling) |
| Volumes | 1.90 GB | 0.41 GB |
| Containers | 0.5 MB | 0.5 MB |

**My recommendation: prune the build cache only** — `docker builder prune -af`. That is 9.3 GB back, and the only cost is that the next Rust and web image builds recompile from scratch instead of hitting cache. Nothing persistent is lost. Adding `docker image prune -f` for the 9 dangling images is nearly as safe and gets you further.

**I would not prune volumes.** There are 30 dangling ones, but they total only 411 MB, and the names on your stopped containers — `vitodnb-postgres`, `yankeybeats-postgres`, `irl-network-postgres` — say some of that is database data from other projects. Bad trade for 411 MB.

Say the word and I will run the build-cache prune. Left alone at this fill level, it will wedge again.

content.text:
Two answers, because the data splits your question in half.

## The backlog is converging, not running away

| week | opened | closed | net | open at end |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| W30 | 122 | 70 | +52 | 52 |
| W31 | 92 | 51 | +41 | 93 |
| W32 | 143 | 120 | **+23** | 116 |

The list does grow. But the growth rate more than halved while the close rate rose from 70 to 120 a week. Last week you closed 120 of 143 opened. That is a queue approaching balance, not one running away. The felt experience of "growing faster" is true of the absolute number and false of the trend.

Where the 116 open issues sit is the more useful fact: **75 are `comp:engine`**. Against that, `comp:api` has 1, `comp:core` has 3, `comp:web` has 16. Track #990 (api) is **fully closed**. Core has 2 left of 15.

## A slice is already testable e2e — today

`tests/web-e2e/tests/smoke.spec.ts` holds 6 real tests, and they run **on pull requests** (`ci.yml:890`, path-filtered on `web`/`e2e`, behind a required result gate). They cover:

- every built login method renders on the front door
- the tab comes under the app-shell service worker
- an unauthenticated deep link lands on the front door
- **a cold start opens a fresh vault at its root**
- signing out returns the tab to the front door
- the login flow leaves nothing outside the storage allow-list

That fourth one is a genuine vertical slice: Web3Auth login → WASM engine boot → vault root resolve → render. It runs against the production static build with the real engine module.

So the honest answer is that the **read path already proves itself end to end.** What does not exist yet is the **write path** in e2e.

## The distance is two issues, and neither is blocked

- **#1096** — extend the web e2e smoke slice to the write path. Its only blocker, #1088, is **closed**. It is launchable now.
- **#642** — rebuild the web shell with login and the vault browser. It has **zero** blockers.

The full cross-client matrix (#651) is further out — it waits on #643 and on desktop #650. But an upload-and-read-back-in-the-browser slice is not gated by anything.

## Why it feels stuck

The engine track absorbs every wave, and it partly feeds itself: engine PRs generate review findings, findings become engine issues, and wave N+1 spends its slots on them. Wave 8 filed nine such issues. That work is real — #1191 and #1187 are latent bricks — but none of it makes the product demonstrable.

**My recommendation: put #1096 at the front of wave 9, ahead of more engine hardening.** It converts "the engine passes its tests" into "the app stores a file and reads it back", which is the thing you cannot currently show anyone. It is unblocked, it is CI work rather than engine work, so it does not contend for the hot files that cap wave parallelism, and it would run in the same PR gate that already guards the read path.

I also corrected a stale memory while checking this: it claimed Web E2E never runs on PRs. That was v1. It runs on v2 PRs now.

```

```

Windows only. I re-ran the failed job and am watching it.

Here is the honest state of the evidence, because it cuts both ways.

**Against the diff being at fault:** it is two files, `net/rotation.rs` and `rotation/reseal.rs`, +59/−40. Neither is on the content read path. The failed test drives `open_content_range` and has nothing to do with re-seal or write-publish classification.

**Against it being a pure flake:** every other `ci.yml` run today passed — twenty of them — *including this same branch at its previous head* `c34e44c35` at 15:08Z. Only the new commit's run failed.

The mechanism that reconciles those is the test's own design. It scans freed memory for a marker byte and asserts the marker is absent. That verdict depends on allocator behaviour, and `content_wipe.rs` links the whole engine library — so **any** change to that library can shift allocation layout and flip the result without the tested code path changing at all. That makes the test sensitive to unrelated edits rather than broken by them.

I am not asserting which it is on one data point. The rerun decides: pass means allocator sensitivity, and #1190 is clean to merge. Fail again means a genuine interaction that deserves triage before merge, and I would want to know why a guard hoist changes what the content assembly buffer leaves behind.

Either way, this looks like a test worth hardening — a required gate that unrelated diffs can flip is a gate that trains people to re-run rather than read.

**Commit 1 — `0c01b4ddc` `refactor: collapse the received-shares store onto a single staging key`** (Closes #1189)
One key holds the whole list. `Slot`, `TargetPreference`, `slot_keys`, `read_slots` and `StoredList.revision` are gone; the body is `encode_stored_list`/`decode_stored_list` over `{shares, v}` and the frozen at-rest byte vector is re-frozen. It stores the self-authenticating contact **code** and re-imports on every load, so host bytes never construct a `Contact`. Only the canonical re-encoding is stored (the offered spelling tolerates unknown fields, so storing it verbatim was an attacker-chosen byte channel). `Full` + `forget` replace the 1024-contact brick; a tampered book now surfaces as `TrustViolation`, not a retryable `Seam`.

15 mutations run, each reverting the guarded production code and watching the named test go red, then restored — including: decode skips an unverifiable code, unreadable book reads as empty, no `Full` check, `forget` drops nothing, code stored verbatim, `resolve_recipient` ignores the identity key, encode allows two codes per identity, `is_bookkeeping` loses the prefix, facade doesn't persist. ### Gates (exit codes)
`cargo fmt --all --check` 0 · `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings` 0 · `cargo test --workspace` 0 · `cargo check -p cipherbox-wasm --target wasm32` 0 · `pnpm typecheck` 0 · `pnpm lint` 0 · `pnpm lint:tracker-refs` 0 · `pnpm test` 0.

## The one thing you need to decide: #1165 is not closed

The review gates found that landing the invite store **as designed is a forgery**, so I held it back rather than ship a latent brick. `RecordedInvite.ephemeral_identity_pk` is bound by nothing — `convert_invite_claim`'s tag re-derivation covers only `ephemeral_enc_pk`. Making `RecordedInvite` host-supplied lets anyone who can write host storage pair a real grantee's public `enc_pk` (which re-derives to that grantee's committed tag) with an identity key they hold, and convert a claim into an owner-signed grant at that grantee's permission — up to `Write`, with no owner key material.

I checked the reviewer's cheap fix (embed the ephemeral half as a contact code) and it does **not** work: a contact code proves "identity A asserts enc E", which an attacker signs for any E. The authority must be the owner's, so the state has to be sealed HPKE-to-self — a new frozen structure tag plus KAT vectors, which is substantially bigger than #1165 describes and deserves its own review. input.content:
## What happened

`Cargo Check & Test (Windows)` failed on PR #1190 at head `28007a12b`:

```
a_mid_read_trust_reject_wipes_what_the_assembly_buffer_already_holds ... FAILED
crates\engine\tests\content_wipe.rs:181: the abandoned assembly buffer reached the allocator unwiped
```

Re-running the same job on the same commit, with no code change, passed. The diff that "caused" it was `crates/engine/src/rotation/reseal.rs` and `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs` — 2 files, +59/-40, nothing on the content read path. Every other `ci.yml` run that day passed, including the same branch at its previous head.

## Why the suite is sensitive to unrelated diffs

`Watchdog` (`crates/engine/tests/content_wipe.rs:42-65`) is a `#[global_allocator]`. While armed, its `dealloc` scans **every** freed block of at least `MARKER_LEN` bytes, process-wide, for a run of the marker byte, and sets `LEAKED` on a hit.

Two consequences follow:

1. The armed window is process-wide, not scoped to the code under test. `watched` (`:78-93`) takes a `SERIAL` mutex, which serialises the scenarios in this binary against each other. It does not stop any other thread in the process from freeing a block inside the window, and every such block is scanned.
2. The verdict depends on allocation layout and timing, not only on whether the production code wiped its buffer. `content_wipe.rs` links the whole engine library, so a change anywhere in that library can shift what is allocated, when it is freed, and what residue a freed block holds — without touching the read path at all.

So a green result is evidence that no marker run reached the allocator on that scheduling, and a red result does not by itself distinguish "the assembly buffer was not wiped" from "some other block freed in the window happened to carry the run". That is the wrong shape for a required gate: it can be flipped by a diff that cannot affect the property being asserted.

Windows failing where Linux and macOS passed fits this reading — a different allocator and CRT produce different residue and different free timing.

## Why it matters beyond one re-run

The gate is required, so the failure blocked a merge. The correct response was a re-run, and a gate whose correct response is "run it again" trains reviewers to re-run rather than read. The next real wipe regression will arrive looking exactly like this one.

## What would fix it

Not decided — options worth weighing:

- Scope the watchdog to allocations the read path actually owns, rather than every `dealloc` in the process, so a foreign block cannot trip it.
- Make a hit report the offending block (size, and where the run starts) instead of a bare boolean, so a failure is diagnosable from CI output alone and a false positive is visible as one.
- Use a marker wide enough that an accidental run is not credible, or verify a hit against the buffer's identity rather than its contents.
- Run the scenarios in a dedicated single-threaded binary if the process-wide window has to stay.

Whatever is chosen, the acceptance condition is that a red result means the wipe failed, and nothing else.

## Repro

Not deterministic. Observed once on `ci.yml` run 31271219451 (Windows leg), passed on re-run of the same commit. Any future occurrence should be added here with its run id.

## The gap

`OwnerScopeKeys` (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:79`) supplies the two per-scope owner derivations every re-seal needs — `writer_pseudonym` and `pointer_read_key`. Both production rotation nets take it as a field and call it on the authoring path:

| Consumer | Field | Call site |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OwnerRotationKeys` | `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:70` | `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:588` |
| the write-wave keys | `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:750` | `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:1301` |

There is **no production implementor**. The only two are `OwnerSeeds` (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:1664`) and `WaveSeeds` (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:3115`), both inside the `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` that opens at `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:1606`. The owner arm of the rotation net is otherwise production code, so this is the one field of it that only a test can fill.

## What is actually undecided

`OwnerSeeds::writer_pseudonym` feeds `kdf::pseudonym_sign` a test constant — `OWNER_ROOT_SECRET: [u8; 32] = [0x6b; 32]` at `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:1657`.

The frozen `pseudonym-sign` edge is `ECDH(ownerEnc, writerEnc) ‖ scopeId (owner: root secret)` (`blueprint/core.md:278`). The grantee half is a real ECDH. The owner half is named only as "root secret", and nothing in the tree binds that phrase to a concrete value: `SessionIdentity` holds `login_secret` (`crates/engine/src/session.rs:46`), `enc_subkey` (`:50`), `owner_pointer_seed` (`:53`) and `identity` (`:58`), and none is designated the pseudonym input.

`SessionIdentity::writer_pseudonym_signer` (`crates/engine/src/session.rs:159`) already composes the edge, but it takes the pairwise material as a parameter and has no caller outside its own unit test. So the composition exists and the input does not.

Picking the owner's input is a KDF-catalog decision — it fixes bytes that every re-sealed structure is signed under and that the adoption gate re-derives — and must not be guessed at inside a facade-wiring PR.

## Checkable condition

- a type outside any `#[cfg(test)]` module and outside the `test-kit` feature implements `OwnerScopeKeys` over `SessionIdentity` alone
- the owner's `pseudonym-sign` input resolves to one named `SessionIdentity` field, and the KDF catalog in `blueprint/core.md` states which one instead of "owner: root secret"
- a record authored through the production owner arm names an `ownerPseudonymPk` that a read-back through the real adoption gate accepts, with the same derivation running on both sides
- the choice is pinned by a KAT vector, so the owner arm's pairwise input cannot drift silently

`Command::RotateNow` (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:504`), `Command::Revoke` (`:474`) and `Command::Downgrade` (`:482`) each need an `OwnerRotationKeys` or the write-wave keys to reach a rotation primitive, and both structs are unconstructible in production until this exists.

TITLE: engine: rebuild the sweep as an interior-node lazy wave over the real seams

## Why this is not wiring

`SweepResolver` (`crates/engine/src/rotation/sweep.rs`) is the last read-plane rotation seam without a production implementation. #1014 landed the other two — `ChildIndexResolver` and `ScopeRootPublisher` — as `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs::OwnerRotationNet`, and deliberately stopped short of this one because it was blocked on a design question rather than on plumbing.

That question is now answered by **[ADR 0003 — Sweep population, and the below-floor descendant scope root](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/blob/main/decisions/0003-sweep-population-and-below-floor-scope-roots.md)** (FSM1/cipher-box-next#58, merged). **Read it before starting.** The answer is not the one the original scope assumed: the resolver could not obtain its work-list because the sweep is walking the wrong population, and the below-floor records it was meant to repair should not be repaired at all.

## What the ADR settles

**The sweep's population is interior nodes, not descendant scope roots.** #26 D2 puts the eager set — the rotated scope root plus every transitively-reachable descendant scope root — under the *cascade*, and gives the sweep the interior nodes that "ride a background sweep re-sealing epoch-lagged nodes". `CONTEXT.md` agrees: epoch lag is "a node whose envelope epoch is behind **its scope's** current epoch". The blueprint's `### sweep` section kept #26 D8's "the work-list is the epoch-lag predicate" and dropped D2's statement of *what* lags, and the implementation followed the blueprint.

**A scope root cannot lag its own floor.** `rotate_scope` and `cascade` both publish first and raise the floor second; `floor::advance_on_unseal` sets the floor equal to the adopted epoch; `minReadEpoch` bumps only on owner read rotations that publish first. So `recordEpoch < floor` on a scope root always means the record fetched is not the current one — most often because the parent's `directChildScopeIndex` names it at a name a `rotateScopeWrite` has since moved. The gate's stage-5 rejection is correct, and the repair is a pointer consult, not a re-seal.

**Consequently the current `sweep_pass` duplicates the cascade with a vacuous predicate.** It enumerates the eager set and calls `reseal_scope_root` — the cascade's job, landed over the real seams in #1053. Nothing it does can fire in production.

## Scope

1. **Re-target the sweep at interior nodes.** Enumerate the nodes *within* a scope from the scope root's read body, stopping at scope-root boundaries (those belong to the cascade), and select those whose envelope epoch is behind the scope's current epoch. Re-seal each under the current node seed at the current epoch via `net::author::author_child_envelope`, and CAS-publish. This replaces the `reseal_scope_root` path in `sweep_pass`, and `SweepTarget` collapses accordingly — an interior node carries no commitment, ledger, grant blobs, or ascent link, so most of the current struct is scope-root material that belongs to the cascade.
2. **Land the concrete resolver over `RecordTransport` + `ApiClient`,** reusing `OwnerRotationNet`'s gated read rather than growing a parallel one. With the population corrected it composes with `gated_root`/the child read path unchanged, because its work-list is drawn from records the adoption gate *accepts*.
3. **Route a below-floor scope root through a pointer consult.** Return a distinct *superseded* verdict — neither `Rejected` (a trust violation) nor `Unavailable` (a transport stall) — and have the handler consult that scope's pointer per #38 D4, re-resolve at the re-pointed `currentRootName`, and fail closed only if the fresh record is still below the floor.
4. **Decouple the index self-heal.** #38 D6's repair is "a scope root encountered but missing from its parent's index is repaired and flagged" — detectable from the enumeration walk alone. Run it on the walk result, independent of any epoch comparison. What is implemented today is canonicalisation performed *during* a lag re-seal, which is both a different repair and unreachable whenever the predicate is vacuous.
5. **Fix the grant-creation convergence gate.** `create_read_grant` (`crates/engine/src/grants/create.rs`) is `sweep_pass`'s only production caller. Its `SubtreeNotConverged` verdict fires only on a lost CAS race, which only happens on a publish, which only happens for a lagging node — so with a vacuous predicate the gate passes unconditionally and "a new grantee cannot regress through an ancestor scope's history" (#26 D2, `CONTEXT.md` "Epoch-converged") is **unenforced today**. Re-targeting the sweep makes the gate able to fire; it needs its own coverage proving it does, including the negative case.

## Definition of done

- [x] `blueprint/engine.md` `### sweep` corrected and `CONTEXT.md` "Lazy wave" tightened — **done in #1066**, so the blueprint is already normative for this work; read it, don't re-derive it
- [ ] ADR 0003 `Status:` flipped to `Accepted — implemented in FSM1/cipher-box#<this PR> (merged)` via a follow-up commit on cipher-box-next, per the ADR 0002 precedent

The blueprint and glossary are maintained **here**, not in cipher-box-next — that repo's `blueprint/` copies are the as-charted archive and must not be edited.

## Gate

- An interior node behind its scope's epoch is re-sealed to the current epoch and published; a node already at the epoch is a no-op. Re-running the pass changes nothing (idempotence), and concurrent sweepers are safe under CAS.
- The walk stops at scope-root boundaries — a descendant scope root inside the subtree is **not** swept, asserted explicitly, so the cascade/sweep split cannot silently regress.
- A below-floor scope root whose pointer re-points to a fresh record converges after the consult; one whose fresh record is still below the floor is refused fail-closed. Distinct, asserted outcomes.
- A forged below-floor record is refused, and no consult path admits it.
- A scope root encountered but absent from its parent's index is repaired and flagged **with no node re-sealed in the same pass**, proving the self-heal no longer rides the epoch comparison.
- Grant creation over a subtree with a lagging interior node refuses with `SubtreeNotConverged`, and succeeds once that node converges — the gate proven live in both directions.
- **The fakes and the concrete impls agree on the same simulation scenarios.** Inherited from #1014's gate, which closed without it (see below).

## Inherited from #1014 — the fake-vs-concrete equivalence check

#1014's gate ended with *"the four fake impls in the testkit and the concrete impls agree on the same simulation scenarios."* It was **unsatisfiable as written** and closed unmet: there are no rotation-seam fakes in `crates/engine/src/testkit/` — every fake is inline in a `#[cfg(test)]` module — and two of the four seams had no concrete impl at the time. #1027, which closed #1014, deferred those two to this issue and #1026 but did not carry the equivalence bullet with them.

It lands here because **this issue is where the last of the four seams gets a production impl**, so the check becomes writable for the first time. Scope:

- run the existing `rotation/` simulation scenarios over the production `SweepResolver` as well as the inline fake, and assert the same outcomes — the pattern `the_eager_set_walk_composes_over_the_production_resolver` (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:2057`) and `the_root_cut_composes_over_the_production_publisher` (`:2090`) already establish
- a fake that has drifted from its production counterpart is a test suite proving nothing, so the divergence must fail a named CI gate, not be discovered by reading

`WriteSubtreeResolver` is the one seam that stays faked after this lands; its production impl is **#1108**, and extending the equivalence check to it belongs there.

## Size

Decided 2026-08-05: **kept whole**, and this issue retitled to match. Scope item 1 is the bulk of it — an interior-node lazy wave needs a new intra-scope walk and a child re-seal path (`net::author::author_child_envelope` exists; the enumeration and the rotation-side wrapper do not), and it invalidates most of the current `SweepTarget`. Items 2–5 are comparatively small once item 1 exists, and they are tightly coupled to it: the resolver's shape, the superseded verdict, and the convergence gate all depend on what the re-target leaves behind. Splitting would have meant a sibling issue whose consumer could not be written until it landed.

## The #1163 decision

`writer_pseudonym_signer` (`session.rs:159`) takes 32 bytes of pairwise material. For a grantee that is `ECDH(ownerEnc, writerEnc)`. For the owner, the frozen catalog says only `(owner: root secret)` — `blueprint/core.md:278` — and nothing binds that phrase to a field. These bytes are what every re-sealed structure is signed under and what the adoption gate re-derives, so the choice is permanent.

`SessionIdentity` offers four fields (`session.rs:43-59`). Options:

1. **`ECDH(ownerEnc, ownerEnc)` — the owner as a degenerate writer.** Self-ECDH over the owner's own encryption subkey. The catalog line loses its parenthetical entirely and becomes uniform: the owner *is* a writer whose `writerEnc` is its own subkey. Only the owner can compute it. No new edge, no new secret, one formula on both sides of the gate. **My recommendation.**
2. **A new dedicated catalog edge**, say `owner-pseudonym-seed`, derived from the login secret through the tree KDF. Cleanest by the one-purpose-one-edge discipline, but it adds a frozen edge and a KAT vector for something option 1 gets free.

4. **`login_secret` directly.** Simplest, and the one I would argue against: it makes the pseudonym a direct function of the master secret, against the narrowest-derived-capability rule that made #789 a crypto HIGH.

content.text:
Good instinct on the ADR — both options amend a frozen catalog line, so either way it needs one. I dug into the code, and **it moved me off option 1.** Here is the reasoning.

## What the code fixes

`enc_subkey` is `derive_key(CTX_ENC_SUBKEY, login_secret)` (`kdf/mod.rs:178`) — a pure function of the login secret, so it never rotates. Both options therefore give a stable per-scope pseudonym. That is not a differentiator.

`pseudonym_sign` takes 32 bytes of pairwise material and a scope id (`kdf/mod.rs:294`). Neither option changes its shape.

## Option 1 — `ECDH(ownerEnc, ownerEnc)`

| Pro | Con |
|---|---|
| Catalog line loses its parenthetical; one formula, no owner special case | Makes the owner's **signing** authority a function of its **encryption** secret |
| No new frozen edge | `diffie_hellman` returns `Option` (`ledger.rs:55`), so it adds a fail-closed branch that cannot fire — an untestable error path |
| Owner becomes a degenerate writer, which reads well in the blueprint | Self-grant collision, below |

## Option 2 — a dedicated `owner-pseudonym-seed` edge

| Pro | Con |
|---|---|
| Signing authority stays independent of the sealing key | The catalog keeps an owner special case |
| One-purpose-one-edge, matching `owner-pointer-seed` next door | Adds a frozen edge |
| Trivial to define: `derive_key(CTX_OWNER_PSEUDONYM_SEED, login_secret)` | |

## The gotchas in option 1 that are not obvious

**The self-grant collision is real, and unguarded.** `create_read_grant` validates the recipient key is usable (`create.rs:315`, `UnusableRecipientKey`) but **never checks that the recipient is not the owner**. The invite path does have that guard — `ClaimantIsTheOwner` in `convert_invite_claim` — so the omission on the direct path is asymmetric. Under option 1, an owner who grants to their own encryption key derives pairwise material identical to their own, so the self-grant's pseudonym *is* the owner's pseudonym. Same principal, so it is not an authority break — but it silently merges two identities the design treats as distinct, and it does so through a path with no guard. Option 2 cannot collide, because the owner's input is not in the grantee's input space at all.

**The key-separation argument is weaker than it first looks, and then stronger again.** A grantee's pseudonym is *already* `ECDH(ownerEnc, writerEnc)`, so grantee signing authority already derives from encryption keys. Option 1 only makes the owner consistent with that. But the owner and a grantee are not symmetric: the owner's `enc_subkey` is the HPKE static sender for op records and the ECDH half against *every* grantee. Compromise it under option 1 and the attacker also holds structure-signing authority for every scope. Compromise a grantee's and they get one grantee's scope. The uniformity is cosmetic; the exposure is not.

## Revised recommendation: option 2

The cost argument I made earlier does not survive contact with the issue text. **#1163 requires a KAT vector either way** — "the choice is pinned by a KAT vector, so the owner arm's pairwise input cannot drift silently". So option 2's only marginal cost over option 1 is one `derive_key` line and one context constant. That is a very small price for keeping the owner's signing authority off its most-exposed secret, and for making the self-grant collision structurally impossible instead of relying on a guard that is currently missing.

I would still file the missing self-grant guard on `create_read_grant` regardless of which option you pick — it is a gap on its own terms.

## On the ADR

Agreed, and it should record more than the choice. The blueprint edit is `blueprint/core.md:278`, replacing `(owner: root secret)`. The ADR belongs in `cipher-box-next/decisions/` because it amends frozen catalog material, and it should carry the rejected option and *why* — specifically that self-ECDH was rejected for key separation and the self-grant collision, so nobody re-proposes the tidier-looking formula later. Same shape as ADR 0003, which #1025 is implementing right now.

Say which option and I will file the ADR, update the catalog line, and brief #1163.

# ADR 0004 — Read-body child names are rewritten by the write-plane name wave

- **Status:** Accepted — implemented in FSM1/cipher-box#1101 (merged)
- **Date:** 2026-08-05
- **Amends:** [#26](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/26) decision D3
  ("Write plane: parallel flat write-seed tree; write rotation = override + child-first
  name wave") — makes concrete what "read-only survivors follow republished mirrors"
  requires, a clause the v2 blueprint dropped
- **Relates to:** [#38](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/38) decision D3
  (the re-point object supplies `currentRootName` only) and
  [#27](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/27) (the child-ref wire format)
- **Implemented by:** [FSM1/cipher-box#1026](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/1026)

## Context

`rotateScopeWrite` mints a fresh write override seed and republishes the scope's whole
subtree under freshly derived names. Every per-node write artefact — `writeSeed`,
`writeKey`, and the Ed25519 IPNS keypair that *is* the `ipnsName` — derives from
`KDF(writeScopeSeed, node.id)`, so a fresh scope seed moves every node in the subtree to
a new name.

D3 of #26 states how each class of party keeps up: "surviving write-grantees derive every
new name locally (zero re-discovery), read-only survivors follow **republished mirrors**
plus the mailbox re-point for the root". #38 D3 later replaced the mailbox with the
owner-signed scope pointer as canonical for the root. The "republished mirrors" half was
never elaborated, and in the v2 blueprint's `### rotateScopeWrite` section it is gone
entirely — the text now reads "read-only survivors follow the owner-signed re-point
object", which covers the root and nothing below it.

That leaves a real hole. A read-only grantee **cannot derive interior names**: the grant
blob carries the write scope seed only for write grants, so a read-only holder has no
`writeScopeSeed` and no way to compute `KDF(writeScopeSeed, node.id)`. The re-point object
carries `currentRootName` and no other name. The only remaining route from the root to a
child is the parent's read-body child list — and `ChildRef` carries an `ipnsName` per
child (#27's wire format). After a name wave those entries name nodes that have moved;
once interior old names batch-retire, they name nothing.

So the wave as specified strands every read-only survivor one level below the root. This
is not an under-implementation of a charted mechanism: no mechanism was ever charted.
The engine's own module text asserts the opposite invariant — "The read plane is
untouched" — which is true of override seeds, read keys and `minReadEpoch`, but not of
read-body *bytes*.

## Decision

**The name wave rewrites read-body child names.** When the wave republishes a node, it
rewrites each `ChildRef.ipnsName` in that node's read body to the child's freshly derived
name and re-seals the read body under the node's unchanged read key at the unchanged read
epoch. The existing child-first ordering already makes every child's new name known
before its parent publishes, so no second pass is needed.

Three consequences follow and are accepted as part of this decision:

1. **The republish is not byte-stable.** The read body changes, so the record cannot be
   reproduced verbatim from its predecessor. Any "carry the read body verbatim" language
   in the blueprint or in `rotateScopeWrite`'s contract is withdrawn.
2. **The publisher needs read-plane material** — the node's read key, and a nonce from
   the entropy seam for the re-seal. The write rotation therefore touches read-plane
   bytes while leaving read-plane *keys and epochs* untouched; the blueprint must say
   the narrower thing rather than "the read plane is untouched".
