# Review-queue handoff

Goal: drive the queued pull requests to **reviewed, green, and ready to merge**.

**Do not merge anything.** The merge decision is the repo owner's and was explicitly
withheld. Leave each pull request ready, with its findings resolved.

## Scripts

```bash
bash cb-chain.sh 1217 1228 1234        # whole queue, one per slot
bash cb-review.sh 1234                 # one pull request
```

`cb-chain.sh` waits for the slot, toggles a stuck-ready pull request, then calls
`cb-review.sh`, which gates on CI, flips ready, polls for the verdict, and leaves
the pull request ready unless inline findings arrive.

Requires `gh` authenticated with write access. Every `gh` call in these scripts is
prefixed `env -u GITHUB_TOKEN` because a stale `GITHUB_TOKEN` in the environment
overrides the keyring credential and fails.

## The one hard constraint

CodeRabbit allows **one review per hour, org-wide**. That, not compute, sets the
pace. Three pull requests take three hours if every verdict is clean.

Anything that puts a new head on a **ready** pull request draws an incremental
review and spends a slot — a push, a rebase, a force-push. Confirmed on #1219: a
one-commit comment fix drew a review 60 seconds later. So:

- Keep a pull request **draft** while you work on it.
- Let `cb-review.sh` re-draft it when findings arrive (it does this automatically).
- Push the fix to the **draft**, then let the chain re-flip it on the next slot.

`gh pr ready` on an already-ready pull request is a no-op, so a refused pull
request needs `gh pr ready --undo` and a re-flip to retrigger.

## Reading a verdict

Three surfaces, and a poller that watches only one reads the other two as silence:

| Verdict | How it appears |
| ------- | -------------- |
| clean | a review on the head with a **zero-length body** |
| findings | a review with a body, plus inline comments |
| refused | a status comment saying "Review limit reached … Next review available in: N minutes" |

A matcher filtering `(.body|length) > 0` discards precisely the clean verdict.

**Nitpicks and "outside the diff range" notes live only inside a collapsible
section of the review body and create NO threads.** Fetch review bodies, not just
`reviewThreads`, or you will not see them.

Establish event order from `repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{n}/timeline`, never from
your own recollection of what happened when.

## Resolving findings

1. **Verify the mechanism before you act.** Read the code the comment names and
   confirm the failure is real. CodeRabbit has a known false-positive rate here;
   several findings this week were retracted after being shown wrong.
2. **Never apply a suggested diff literally.** Treat it as a symptom report, not a
   specification. Applying suggestions verbatim has twice produced a worse bug
   than the one reported.
3. Reply on the thread saying what was done and why, then resolve it.
4. **Post a disposition comment** covering every nitpick and out-of-scope item —
   taken, already true, rejected with the reason, or deferred to a named issue. A
   blanket "addressed the feedback" is not a disposition. This is a standing rule
   (`.claude/commands/resolve-pr-reviews.md`), and it is the step that gets
   dropped, because nitpicks leave no thread to remind you.
5. File a follow-up issue for anything real you do not fix, with labels
   `v2-build` and the right `comp:` label, milestone `v2.0.0`, and a parent via
   the sub-issues API.

### Findings you should REJECT

`AGENTS.md` forbids these, so a comment asking for one is wrong:

- **Absence-justifying comments** — prose explaining why a path *not* in the code
  cannot happen.
- **Unchanged-code apologia** — a doc block defending code the diff does not touch.
- **Bare tracker references in code** (`#1234`) — `pnpm lint:tracker-refs` is a
  merge-blocking gate. State the condition instead.

Say so on the thread with the rule cited. Do not silently skip.

## Gates before any push

Run each **bare** and read `$?` directly. Do not pipe a gate through `tail`, `tee`
or `head` — under zsh `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` is empty, so you read the pipe's status
and a red gate reports green.

```
cargo fmt --all -- --check          # --all, never scoped to -p; the CI gate is --all
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test --workspace
cargo check -p cipherbox-wasm --target wasm32-unknown-unknown   # --workspace never builds wasm32
pnpm lint:tracker-refs
```

Never share `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` between worktrees — it yields stale test binaries
and identical pass counts that hide a failure.

## Repo rules

- **Never push to `main`.** Feature branches and pull requests only.
- **No tool attribution anywhere** — no "Generated with" line, no `Co-Authored-By`
  naming an assistant, no session link, in commits, pull request titles, bodies,
  issues, or review comments. Strip it if your harness adds it, and check the
  rendered body afterwards.
- Conventional Commits, and **no parentheses in a pull request title** — it breaks
  Release Please.
- Comments explain **why**, briefly, stated once at their home.
- Encode/decode fail-closed symmetry: an invariant the decode path hard-rejects
  needs a **release-active** encode-side check returning `Err`, never
  `debug_assert!`, which is stripped in release.
- All crypto lives in `crates/core`. TypeScript has no crypto of its own.
- Never write a closing keyword to negate it — "does not close #1165" **still**
  auto-closes the issue.

## Queue state at handoff (2026-08-09, ~10:30Z)

| PR | State | Notes |
| -- | ----- | ----- |
| #1217 | ready, mid-review | `fix(engine): settle a refused upload …` |
| #1228 | draft | `chore(ci): set KUBO_API_URL for staging …` |
| #1234 | draft | owner-local sealed stores; closes #1207, #1233, #1239; **must NOT close #1165 or #1240** |

Verify each before acting — these will have moved.

**On #1234 specifically:** its body says `Advances #1165`. Leave that wording
exactly as it is. #1165 stays open because two of its four checkable conditions
need a facade mint path that does not exist; that work is #1240.

content.text:
Three files sent. Both scripts pass `bash -n` and the date helpers are portable — they try GNU `date -d` first and fall back to BSD, since the web box is almost certainly Linux and the originals were macOS-only.

**`cb-chain.sh 1217 1228 1234`** waits for the slot, toggles a stuck-ready PR, and hands off. **`cb-review.sh <PR>`** gates on CI, flips, polls, and leaves the PR ready unless inline findings arrive.

**`BRIEF.md` is the part that matters.** The scripts only do the toggling; the resolution judgment is all in the brief. It carries the traps that cost real slots today: a clean verdict is a **zero-length** review body, so a `(.body|length) > 0` filter discards exactly what it seeks; nitpicks create no threads, so `reviewThreads` alone cannot see them; and any new head on a *ready* PR draws an incremental review and spends a slot. Plus the disposition-comment rule, the reject-these-findings list, and the bare-`$?` gate discipline.

**State changed while I was writing it, so the brief reflects the real position:**

- **#1217's verdict landed at 10:24:06Z** — `Actionable comments posted: 1`. It re-drafted itself automatically.
- **The next slot opens 11:26:06Z.**
- Fixing #1217 costs no slot; only the re-flip afterwards does. So the efficient order is fix #1217 first, then run the chain — and the brief says so.

Realistically that is three flips in the next three hours, so the queue can be fully reviewed by roughly 13:30Z if verdicts stay clean. Each PR that comes back with findings costs a second slot.

Two things I deliberately did not put in the scripts: **nothing merges**, and nothing re-drafts on a *failed poll* — a late verdict still lands on a ready PR, whereas re-drafting forces a re-flip at merge time and burns a slot. That inversion is what got #1215 refused this morning.

The one thing to sanity-check on the other side is that `gh` is authenticated with write access. If it can only read, the chain will fail at the flip and exit 5 rather than doing anything silently wrong.

ci: extend the web e2e smoke slice to the write path

## Goal

Extend the `Web E2E Smoke` slice to the write path, so the merge gate covers the
folder-CRUD and upload/download half that `blueprint/testing.md` scopes into the
PR tier ("a bounded-minutes budget of web login-and-CRUD").

The slice landed in #1078 covers login, the read path, and sign-out only. Of the
three things that blocked the write path when this was filed, **one remains**,
and it does not belong to the suite.

## The blocker

**No pin store under the smoke job.** `.github/workflows/web-e2e.yml:29-31`
declares one service, Postgres; the mock `/routing/v1` record store is started as
a workflow step at `:112-122`. There is no Kubo and no `KUBO_API_URL` anywhere in
the file. The API pins hosted uploads through `KuboPinStore`, whose `rpc()` throws
`ServiceUnavailableException('Hosted pin store not configured')` when
`KUBO_API_URL` is unset (`apps/api/src/registry/pin-store.ts`), so
`POST /content/upload` answers 503.

The engine does not classify a 503: `classify_upload` returns
`Halt::Unclassified` for any non-413 status, and `apply_valve` charges no attempt
for `Halt::Unclassified` (`crates/engine/src/sync/drain.rs`). The op therefore
retries forever instead of dead-lettering, and the upload row sits at phase
`stalled` ("retrying"). **An upload spec written today would hang to the 120s test
timeout rather than fail** — worth knowing before anyone adds one.

This also blocks folder create: the record head block goes through the same
`/content/upload` before the register-first CAS publish
(`crates/engine/src/net/record_publish.rs`).

## Cleared blockers

The two chrome blockers this issue originally recorded are gone:

- **CRUD affordances ship.** `apps/web/src/components/file-browser/FileBrowserActions.tsx:63-74`
  builds preview / download / rename / move / details / delete context items, and
  `:88` carries a `new-folder-button` testid. Landed with #806 / #1081.
- **The download affordance ships.** `useFileDownload` is constructed at
  `FileBrowserActions.tsx:44` and invoked at `:65`. Landed with #807 / #1081.

Specs still bind to `data-testid`s, so check the shipped testids rather than
inventing new ones.

## Work

- Add an `ipfs/kubo` service plus `KUBO_API_URL` to `.github/workflows/web-e2e.yml`,
  mirroring the contract job in `ci.yml`. This is the whole of what makes any
  write assertion possible.
- Scoped folder create / rename / move / delete specs against the shipped testids.
- Upload-then-download round trip asserting the bytes survive.
- Correct `tests/web-e2e/README.md`: the "No affordance to drive" bullet
  (`:25-28`) is already false and should go now; the "No pin store under the job"
  bullet (`:29-34`) and the section heading go when the Kubo service lands.

`retries: 0` stays policy — a flaky write spec is a defect, not a tuning problem.

Because that constructor **copies** when handed a non-buffer, the existing scrub was zeroing the copy and leaving the sender's plaintext intact — a wipe that looked correct and did nothing. PR B is up as draft **[#1242](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/pull/1242)**, all gates green — but it needs a ruling from you, and the agent was right to escalate rather than decide.

**It implemented #1175 in TypeScript using WebCrypto, which is a carve-out from `AGENTS.md` rule 4** ("all crypto lives in `crates/core` — TypeScript has no crypto of its own").

I checked the actual surface before forming a view. It is three calls: `generateKey` (AES-GCM 256, `extractable: false`), `encrypt`, `decrypt` — an AES-GCM wrap of an opaque blob under a browser-held key, with AAD binding it to its storage key. **No KDF, no codec, no wire format, no KAT.**

**My reading: ratify it.** Rule 4 exists so there is one implementation of the *protocol* and one KAT set. This is key custody, not protocol crypto, and it introduces neither. More decisively, the agent's central argument holds — non-extractability is a property only a WebCrypto-held key can have. A Rust/WASM version would necessarily materialise the key bytes in linear memory, destroying the exact control #1175 exists to gain. So "move it to `crates/core`" is not a stricter option, it is a broken one.

If you agree, rule 4 should gain a sentence naming the exception — browser-held key custody, no protocol material, no derivation — so the next reviewer does not re-litigate it. **The agent explicitly declined to edit `AGENTS.md` itself**, on the grounds that declaring a policy carve-out is not a subagent's call. That was the right instinct.

Two other things worth your attention:

**It corrected #1175's threat model in the code.** The issue claims a copied profile is covered. It is not — `extractable: false` bars export to script, not presence on disk, so a whole-profile copy carries the IndexedDB key with it. The stated benefit was overstated.

**It fixed #1236 one level deeper than the issue specified.** Rather than the prescribed hook-side `onStreamError` subscription, the failure now rides on `whenIdle`'s own result. It built the prescribed version first, then changed course — which removed a hook-side latch that could never clear once a ticket re-opened, and would have reported a *recovered* save as failed. `save` returns `'saved' | 'refused' | 'failed'`.

Three deliberate breaks **failed to fail**, and it treated that as the code being wrong rather than the test — removing two unreachable guards and rewriting the third test, which then caught it.

Waiting on A and D. Say the word on the rule-4 carve-out and I will draft the `AGENTS.md` amendment.

`useFileDownload` mints a `/stream/<ticket>` URL and clicks an anchor. The Service Worker does not intercept that request, so the origin answers it with the SPA fallback. The user receives a **394-byte `index.html` named `notes.txt`**, and nothing reports a failure.

Silent data corruption at the moment a member takes their file out of the product. It fails closed on neither side: no error to the user, no dead letter, no telemetry.

ok I am busy doing some UAT on #1246

"The Service Worker download path — whether an ordinary browser saves the file or the app shell. It's the one claim from #1246 I could only establish inside Playwright, and CI can't settle it because Playwright's own download capture is the suspect.

Setup. pnpm dev at localhost:5173 is fine; the worker registers in dev too (/src/sw.ts as a module, /sw.js classic in a build). Sign in, upload a small text file.

Before clicking anything, check DevTools → Application → Service Workers and confirm one is activated and controlling this page. This is the step that makes the test meaningful: if it isn't controlling, MediaService.streaming is false, streamTicket returns null, and useFileDownload.save quietly takes the buffered blob path — which works correctly and would tell you nothing about the path under suspicion.

Then, with the Network tab open and filtered to stream, preview the file and click download (the row's action menu works too — both call downloads.save).

Three observations, in order of how decisive they are:

The /stream/<ticket> request. Served (from ServiceWorker) means the pipe answered and the path is healthy. Answered by the dev server with an HTML body means the request bypassed the worker — that's the failure.
The saved file. Your text, or the app's index.html.
Roughly 30 seconds after the click, if the worker never saw the fetch, whenStreamIdle(ticket, 30_000) resolves false and the UI surfaces "the browser did not start the download" (NEVER_FETCHED in useFileDownload.ts, rendered via downloads.error). A spurious error there is corroboration on its own.
If it reproduces, two things are wrong, and the second is the worse one: the member saves the wrong bytes, and the ticket — a bearer capability to plaintext, per createStreamUrl's own comment — has been sent to the origin server. If it doesn't reproduce, the cause is Playwright's CDP download capture, the finding is a harness limitation rather than a product defect, and nothing needs changing.

Either way #1246 is unaffected: its byte assertion no longer goes anywhere near that path."

Two things worth having before you interpret the result.

**A dev-server pass would not clear it.** The web-e2e suite runs against the **production static build**, which is where the failure was observed — and by your own note the worker registers differently in the two modes (`/src/sw.ts` as a module in dev, `/sw.js` classic in a build). A module worker registered from a Vite-served path is a different registration, with different scope resolution, than the classic one the built bundle ships. So a clean `pnpm dev` run leaves the suspect path untested. If it does not reproduce, it is worth one repeat against `pnpm build` + preview before concluding harness.

**#1247 is currently overstated, and that is my error.** I filed it asserting a product defect on the strength of "reproduced 3/3", without registering that all three reproductions were inside Playwright with its own download capture in the loop — which is exactly the confound this protocol exists to remove. The issue body states the SPA-fallback save as established fact. If your UAT clears it, I will rewrite it as a harness limitation against the Playwright download path; if it confirms, I will add your observations as the independent reproduction it currently lacks.

**One addition that decides the security half independently of the bytes.** The two failures are separable: the member saving wrong bytes, and the ticket reaching the origin. The second is the worse one and does not depend on what the browser did with the response. Check the dev server's request log for the `/stream/<ticket>` path — if the origin logged the ticket at all, the bearer capability left the client, and that holds even if the download otherwise looks fine. That is a zero-knowledge violation on its own terms, so it deserves its own issue rather than riding on #1247.

Your read on #1246 matches mine: its byte assertion goes through the buffered `facade.download` preview path, so none of this touches it either way.

content.text:
You are right on both counts, and v1 proves it rather than my having to argue it.

**v1's identity plane had one shape for every method** — `useAuth.ts:479-480` states it outright:

> Google idToken → CipherBox backend → CipherBox JWT → Core Kit `loginWithJWT` → backend `/auth/login` (corekit type)

Wallet used that same path. `WalletLoginButton.tsx:72-81` fetches a nonce, signs SIWE, calls `identityWalletVerify`, and receives **`{ idToken, userId }`** — a CipherBox-issued JWT — which then went to Core Kit `loginWithJWT`. The API's own `walletVerifyDtoIntent` says it plainly: `login` "creates/finds a user", `link` "only verifies ownership". Wallet was a first-class first login.

**So the premise under #910 and #938 is false.** "SIWE cannot produce the Core Kit login secret" is not a property of the architecture — it is a consequence of how v2 wired the client. `apps/web/src/auth/coreKit.ts:59` calls **`loginWithOAuth`**, and there is no `loginWithJWT` anywhere in v2. Once the only door is Web3Auth's own OAuth, any method that authenticates against CipherBox first has no way in, and SIWE gets rationalised as "secondary" to fit the wiring rather than the design.

**And your second point lands the same way.** v1 had `apps/api/src/auth/services/email-otp.service.ts` with `sendOtpDto`/`verifyOtpDto` — CipherBox owned passwordless email. v2's API auth directory has **no email-otp service and no SendGrid reference at all**; `siwe.service.ts` survived, the OTP service did not. So passwordless email in v2 is Web3Auth's, not ours.

This is a regression in the identity plane, not two separate UI bugs. The correct fix is to restore the CipherBox-JWT → `loginWithJWT` path, which recovers wallet-as-first-login and lets the API own passwordless email again — and that makes #938 wrong as written, since it proposes moving the wallet button off the login page to accommodate a limitation that should not exist.

v2 authenticates the Core Kit only through Web3Auth's own OAuth flow, so any method that authenticates against CipherBox first has no way to produce a login secret. v1 did not work this way. The consequence has been mistaken for a property of the design, and two issues now rest on it.

## What v1 did

**CipherBox was the identity provider.** Every method converged on one shape (`apps/web/src/hooks/useAuth.ts` on branch `v1`):

```
<method> -> CipherBox backend -> CipherBox JWT -> Core Kit loginWithJWT -> /auth/login (corekit type)
```

`completeBackendAuth`'s own doc states the reason: "Sends the CipherBox-issued JWT (which we used for Core Kit `loginWithJWT`) to the backend with loginType 'corekit'. The backend verifies it against its own JWKS **since CipherBox is the identity provider**."

That held for Google (`:479-480`), for email OTP (`:540-543`), and for wallet.

**Wallet was a first-class first login.** `apps/web/src/components/auth/WalletLoginButton.tsx:72-81` fetches a nonce, signs a SIWE message, calls `identityWalletVerify`, and receives `{ idToken, userId }` — a CipherBox-issued JWT — which then goes to Core Kit `loginWithJWT`. The API's own contract says so: `walletVerifyDtoIntent` documents `login` as "creates/finds a user" and `link` as "only verifies ownership". Two intents, because logging in with a wallet was one of them.

**CipherBox owned passwordless email.** `apps/api/src/auth/services/email-otp.service.ts`, with `sendOtpDto` / `verifyOtpDto`.

## What v2 does

`apps/web/src/auth/coreKit.ts:59` calls **`loginWithOAuth`**. There is no `loginWithJWT` anywhere in `apps/web`, and no path from a CipherBox-issued token into the Core Kit.

`apps/api/src/auth/services/` kept `siwe.service.ts` and dropped the OTP service; there is no SendGrid reference in `apps/api` at all. So passwordless email is Web3Auth's, not ours, and SIWE authenticates an account that no longer has a door into the key plane.

## Why this matters beyond two buttons

- **Wallet cannot be a first login**, so the affordance on the login page dead-ends in `NotStarted`. Confirmed by hand against the local stack.
- **Passwordless email is delegated**, so the member's email flow, its deliverability, its rate limits and its branding are outside CipherBox.
- **The identity provider moved.** In v1 the account's identity was anchored on a CipherBox JWT verified against CipherBox's own JWKS. In v2 it is anchored on Web3Auth's OAuth. That is an architectural change, and it does not appear to have been decided anywhere — it reads as a consequence of the client wiring.

## Work

- Restore the CipherBox-JWT path into the Core Kit (`loginWithJWT` against a CipherBox verifier), so a method that authenticates to the API can mint a login secret.
- Reinstate the API-owned passwordless email OTP, with its provider configured rather than assumed.
- Return SIWE to a first-login method, driven by the existing `siwe.service.ts` plus the nonce/verify pair and the `login` / `link` intents v1 already specified.

Harvest reference on branch `v1`: `hooks/useAuth.ts`, `components/auth/WalletLoginButton.tsx`, `components/auth/LinkedMethods.tsx`, `apps/api/src/auth/services/{siwe,email-otp}.service.ts`.

Known hazard, already hit once: `.learnings/2026-02-16-ephemeral-jwks-web3auth-caching.md` on `v1` records a JWKS caching failure in exactly this handoff.

## Consequences for open issues

- **#938** proposes moving the wallet button off the login page onto a started-engine surface. That accommodates the limitation instead of removing it, and should not be built as written.
- **#910** gated `facade.siweChallenge` on a started engine on the same premise.

Neither is wrong about the code as it stands; both are wrong about why it stands that way.

## Acceptance

- A member with no prior session signs in with a wallet and reaches a working vault.
- A member with no prior session signs in with an emailed one-time code delivered by CipherBox.
- The Core Kit login secret derives from a CipherBox-issued JWT verified against CipherBox's JWKS.
- The wallet affordance on the login page no longer dead-ends.
EOF

content.text:
The blueprint already agrees with you — and it also names the one thing that cannot move.

**`blueprint/web-client.md` "Login and identity" is explicit on both halves:**

> **Web3Auth Core Kit runs on the UI thread** (it owns its DOM/redirect flows, MFA enrollment, and device approval — all UI-side, outside the engine's sight).

> **The engine owns the token lifecycle** (FSM1/cipher-box-next#28 D5): challenge-signature login through its API client; access JWT in engine memory; refresh cookie rides the Http seam.

So engine-owned orchestration is not a change of direction — it is what was specified and not built. What must stay in TypeScript is narrow and unavoidable: the Core Kit SDK itself (it is a JS SDK with redirect flows and MFA UI) and wagmi collecting the wallet signature. Everything else — nonce, verify, OTP send/verify, the JWT exchange, token refresh, method linking — is API orchestration the engine should own, and today none of it lives there.

**There is a sequencing problem you will hit immediately, and it is the thing to decide before scoping.** v1's order is:

```
method → API → CipherBox JWT → Core Kit loginWithJWT → login secret → engine start(secret)
```

The API exchange happens **before** the engine has a secret to start with. But today the facade refuses everything pre-start — `command()` returns `NotStarted`, and #910 gated `siweChallenge` the same way. So "the engine owns the token lifecycle" cannot cover the part that must run first, unless the engine gains an **identity phase that works unstarted**: a surface that can talk to the API, hand the host a CipherBox JWT, take back the exported login secret, and only then cold-start the vault.

That is a change to the facade's contract, not an implementation detail, and it is the thing that makes this span all four layers coherently rather than four separate patches.

**Second decision it forces:** if the engine orchestrates, it must *ask* the host to run the Core Kit step. That is a callback into the host — and this repo has ruled against adding seams lightly, on the grounds that `SeamSet`'s field-struct construction is a compile-time completeness gate and a new seam breaks every implementor. The invite store was kept off a tenth seam for exactly that reason. Worth deciding deliberately whether identity earns one or rides an existing surface.

**My recommendation: write the ADR before the code.** Two decisions, both cross-cutting and both expensive to reverse once four layers depend on them — the pre-start identity phase, and how the engine reaches the Core Kit. Then #1253's work breaks down cleanly per layer, and the Tauri webview gets the same orchestration for free, which is the actual payoff.

Want me to draft it? I would scope it to those two decisions and leave the per-layer work to #1253.

What specifically prevented sharing:

1. **React-shaped web code.** `useAuth.ts` is a 732-line hook coupled to Zustand stores, `react-router`'s `navigate`, and five other stores. Desktop's webview is vanilla TS (`main.ts` builds DOM by hand) with no React and no stores.
2. **The Rust handoff.** Desktop's terminal step is `invoke('handle_auth_complete', { idToken, privateKey })` (`src/auth.ts:345-348`); web's is `setVaultKeys()` into a Zustand store. Post-auth on desktop means FUSE mount + sync daemon + tray (`commands/auth.rs:165-311`), which has no web analogue.
3. **Different transports for the same endpoints** (cookie vs body refresh token), forced by the API's `x-client-type` branch.
4. **Different provider entry points for Google** (§3).

None of these are Core Kit limitations. Core Kit itself ran fine in the Tauri webview — same SDK, same verifier `'cipherbox-identity'`, same `window.localStorage` storage, same `_UNSAFE_exportTssKey`, MFA/REQUIRED_SHARE/device-approval all functional.

Two halves of one login flow pointed at two different API hosts. Fixed with `option_env!` in `main.rs`.

### 3. The redirect problem

From `.planning/debug/resolved/google-oauth-tauri-redirect.md` plus `commands/oauth.rs`:

- **What broke.** Desktop cannot use GIS One Tap — the doc's own evidence entry states "GIS doesn't work in Tauri webview" (no Google session, unregistered origin), so desktop fell back to a manual OAuth2 implicit flow, which *requires* a `redirect_uri`. `getGoogleCredential()` built it from `window.location.origin`. In production Tauri builds that origin is `tauri://localhost` on macOS (`https://tauri.localhost` on Windows — `oauth.rs:75-77`), so the request carried `redirect_uri=tauri://localhost/google-callback.html`. Google validates `redirect_uri` server-side and rejects any non-`http(s)` scheme → `Error 400: invalid_request`. Dev mode worked (origin was `http://localhost:1420`), so this only manifested in packaged builds.
- **The solution.** `start_oauth_server` (`oauth.rs:91-134`) binds a short-lived Tokio TCP listener on `127.0.0.1`, trying fixed pre-registered ports `[14200, 14201, 14202]` (`oauth.rs:62`) and failing fast rather than falling back to a random port (RFC 8252 allows `http://localhost` with dynamic ports for native clients, but a random port can't be pre-registered in Google Console). It serves a callback HTML page carrying a random 16-byte nonce (`oauth.rs:119-124, 142-181`); Google's implicit-flow fragment is unreadable server-side, so that page extracts `#id_token=` in JS and POSTs it to `/token`; the server validates the nonce (`oauth.rs:320-324`), emits a port-scoped Tauri event `oauth-callback-{port}`, and shuts down. Absolute 120 s deadline (`oauth.rs:219`). The frontend listens for that event and validates OAuth `state` before accepting (`src/auth.ts:750-755`).
- **A second, separate Tauri problem** is also solved there: `open_oauth_popup` (`oauth.rs:19-51`) creates the popup as a Tauri `WebviewWindow` from Rust because `window.open()` is unreliable on Windows WebView2. It host-allowlists `accounts.google.com` over HTTPS only (`oauth.rs:28-35`).

**Worth keeping (evidence-backed):**

- **The token seam.** `getAccessToken: () => Promise<string>` as the *only* identity-facing input to the shared runtime is the one boundary that held up with zero churn across both hosts and never appears in any debug doc. Both `packages/sdk` and `packages/sdk-core` stayed identity-free for the whole of v1.
- **Rust owning the post-auth secret lifecycle on desktop.** Keychain storage, `Zeroizing` on the private key, and `state.clear_keys()` on logout (`commands/auth.rs:99, 504`) are structurally better than the web's `Uint8Array.fill(0)` in a Zustand store (`auth.store.ts:72-81`).
- **Provider-agnostic backend contract.** The CipherBox API acting as its own identity provider — `/auth/identity/{google,email,wallet}` mints a CipherBox JWT, then Core Kit `loginWithJWT` with a single verifier `'cipherbox-identity'` — meant all three methods converged on one code path immediately after credential collection. Both hosts adopted it identically. This is the natural join point.

**Incidental / accidental:**

- The web/desktop split of Core Kit orchestration itself. It produced two implementations of one algorithm that measurably drifted: network map (MAINNET vs DEVNET), the device-factor auto-recovery branch present only in web (`hooks.ts:204-234`), hand-concatenated SIWE on desktop vs `viem/siwe` on web, and the API-URL mismatch bug above.

- Desktop's device-identity scheme (random localStorage value, `platform: 'macos'` hardcoded) — divergence with no design rationale visible in the code.
- The cookie-vs-body refresh-token fork. Driven by the browser XSS threat model, not by anything about desktop; it forced an `x-client-type` header branch in the API and two separate refresh implementations.

**Not established** (no evidence found either way):

- Whether the desktop wallet path was ever removed deliberately or just abandoned mid-phase — the only signal is a code comment deferring WalletConnect to "Phase 11" (`src/auth.ts:190`).
- Whether GIS was ever actually attempted in the Tauri webview and observed failing, versus assumed to fail. The debug doc asserts it as evidence but cites no reproduction.
- Any explicit ADR justifying "auth stays in the app, not a package." `.planning/adr/002-web3auth-mfa.md` exists but I did not find a package-boundary decision; the boundary appears to be emergent rather than decided.</result>

v1's facts are in, and they are more decisive than I expected.

**v1 shared zero login code.** No package under `packages/` contains any auth logic — a grep across `sdk`, `sdk-core`, `core` and `crypto` returns only incidental comments. The duplication was roughly **3,600 lines in web against 2,400 in desktop**, implementing the same flows twice.

**The boundary was deliberate, and it was drawn at the bearer token.** `packages/sdk` took `getAccessToken: () => Promise<string>`, and `sdk-core` took `SdkContext { apiUrl, getAccessToken }`. Both were pure token *consumers*. Everything that **produced** the token — provider SDKs, Core Kit, TSS export, vault bootstrap — sat above the shared runtime and was therefore per-host by construction.

**That boundary is in the wrong place, and v1 paid for it in measurable drift:**

- web mapped `production → MAINNET`, desktop mapped `production → DEVNET`
- web had a device-factor auto-recovery branch desktop lacked
- web used `viem/siwe`; desktop hand-concatenated the EIP-4361 string
- desktop's wallet login was written, never wired, never exercised
- and one real bug: email OTP worked in web and broke in packaged desktop because the JS half read `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL` at compile time while the Rust half read `std::env::var` at runtime — two halves of one login flow pointing at different API hosts

**The Core Kit is not the obstacle.** It ran fine in the Tauri webview — same SDK, same `cipherbox-identity` verifier, same storage, MFA and device approval functional. So "Core Kit must stay in TS" does not imply "login must be per-host".

**Exactly one thing is genuinely host-specific: Google credential collection.** Google Identity Services does not work in the Tauri webview, so desktop fell back to a manual OAuth2 implicit flow, which needs a `redirect_uri` — and a packaged Tauri app's origin is `tauri://localhost`, which Google rejects as a non-`http(s)` scheme. v1 solved it with a loopback server on pre-registered ports 14200–14202 serving a callback page. Dev builds worked and only packaged builds broke, which is why it was found late.

**The agent's own read on the join point matches the shape of #1253**: the CipherBox API acting as its own identity provider, with all three methods converging on one path immediately after credential collection, is "the natural join point" — and it is the one thing both hosts adopted identically.

So the evidence points at moving the boundary **one step earlier than v1 drew it**: per-host credential *collection* only, with everything after it shared. Whether "shared" means TypeScript in a package or Rust in the engine is what the second analysis decides — it is inventorying `packages/client`'s browser assumptions now.

| `refresh()` — single-flight rotation, coalesced waiters, tears down session on failure | refresh endpoint | `:247-283` |
| `logout()` — server-side revoke + `clear_session()` | `POST /auth/logout` | `:285-296` |
| `is_authenticated()` | — | `:120-122` |

Facade level: `Engine::start(secret: LoginSecret)` at `crates/engine/src/facade.rs:1699` derives `SessionIdentity` purely from the secret (`:1716`), then calls `api.login_identity(&signer)` fail-closed before committing the session (`:1727-1731`), then drops/zeroizes the secret at its terminal owner (`:1750`). `LoginSecret` (`facade.rs:315-340`) is `Zeroizing`, no `Clone`, `Debug` prints `LoginSecret(redacted)`, and `expose()` is `pub(crate)`. `ApiBaseUrl::parse` refuses a blank origin so a shipped host cannot start unauthenticated (`facade.rs:381`). `Engine::siwe_challenge()` is a facade method at `facade.rs:2983`; `Command::SiweLogin { message, signature }` and `Command::Logout` at `facade.rs:522-530`. Desktop seams for auth already exist in Rust: `crates/desktop-seams/src/credential_store.rs` — `KeyringCredentialStore` (OS keyring, refresh token + last-account id only, `lib.rs:11-12`).

**What is left in TypeScript is:** the Core Kit SDK adapter, wagmi/viem signature collection, and the `useAuth` state machine that sequences them.

## 4. What the blueprints say

`blueprint/desktop.md` (313 lines). Critical negative results: **`packages/client` appears 0 times; `react` 0 times; `wasm` 0 times; `apps/web` 0 times.**

`desktop.md:91-96` — the load-bearing passage:

> The facade is called directly (in-process async Rust) — no RPC layer, no worker, no tab leadership; the single-writer invariant is free on desktop because there is exactly one engine per running app. The Tauri webview is login-and-settings chrome only: it renders facade state forwarded over Tauri events and never holds tokens or keys (the v1 `handle_auth_complete` handoff survives, but the secret goes straight to `start(secret)` and is zeroized).

`desktop.md:246-252` — the login split:

> **Login**: Web3Auth Core Kit in the webview (its DOM/redirect flows, MFA, device approval — all chrome-side); the exported secret crosses to `start(secret)` once and is zeroized. Challenge-signature login, token refresh, and session restore are engine-native (engine.md API client); the shell's only credential duty is hosting the keychain seam. Dev-key mode survives: a debug flag feeds the staging test-login path through the same facade, keychain bypassed — the headless agent/e2e seam.

`desktop.md:21-24` — native linking, not WASM:

> The desktop app is the engine's **native host**: `apps/desktop` links `crates/engine` directly in the Tauri process and owns login, lifecycle, tray, and updater

`desktop.md:192-194` — vault UI is delegated to the web app:

> The bin is not projected into the mount in v2.0; restore/purge live in the web UI and the tray's "Open CipherBox".

The only TS mention in the whole file is a deletion (`desktop.md:36`: *"The desktop twin engine … and its TS divergence table | #28 D1 — one Rust engine, linked natively"*). SIWE/wagmi appear **nowhere** in desktop.md.

`blueprint/web-client.md` (284 lines). **`desktop` appears 0 times.**

`web-client.md:11-15` scopes it to *"the three **web-side** units … `crates/wasm`, `packages/client`, `apps/web`"*. `web-client.md:50-54` defines the package:

> **`packages/client`** — everything between the WASM boundary and React: engine worker lifecycle, tab leadership, the two facade transports, every browser seam implementation (IndexedDB, OPFS, `fetch`), the login handoff, and the Service Worker brokerage. It wraps the facade, never extends it; it holds no vault semantics.

`web-client.md:189-201` states the same TS/Rust split as desktop:

> **Web3Auth Core Kit runs on the UI thread** (it owns its DOM/redirect flows, MFA enrollment, and device approval — all UI-side, outside the engine's sight)… **The engine owns the token lifecycle** (#28 D5): challenge-signature login through its API client; access JWT in engine memory; refresh cookie rides the Http seam. SIWE stays secondary — wagmi collects the wallet signature on the UI thread and the facade forwards it.

Note the one place where the hosts genuinely diverge in the same seam: web's `CredentialStore` is a **no-op** because the refresh token is an HTTP-only cookie carried by `credentials: 'include'` (`web-client.md:153,158`), while desktop's is the OS keyring (`desktop.md:89`).

## 5. Practical sharing verdict (facts only)

If login orchestration stayed in TypeScript, **there is nothing to share it *with* today.** `apps/desktop/frontend` is a 43-line static HTML file with no bundler, no TypeScript, no `dependencies`, and no engine binding. Sharing would require first *creating* a desktop frontend app — and then a place to put the shared code, since `apps/web/src/auth/**` is app-local and there is no second JS consumer in the repo.

Concrete obstacles, evidenced:

1. **No desktop JS app exists.** No vite config, no tsconfig, no `src/`, no `dependencies` in `apps/desktop/package.json`; `tauri.conf.json` has no `beforeBuildCommand`. This would be new build config, not a refactor.
2. **No engine binding on desktop.** `src-tauri/Cargo.toml` does not depend on `crates/engine`; `main.rs:3` says "no engine wiring, no login". The `useAuth` orchestration calls `client.facade.{start,siweChallenge,siweLogin,logout}` — on desktop those would be Tauri IPC commands that do not exist yet. **The transport under the orchestration is not the same object on both hosts**, so the shared unit would have to be parameterised over it.
3. **`packages/client` is not the vehicle.** It is defined as one of the *three web-side units* (`web-client.md:11-15`) and its entire non-type surface assumes Workers, `navigator.locks`, `BroadcastChannel`, `navigator.serviceWorker`, IndexedDB, OPFS. `desktop.md:91-93` explicitly rules its machinery out on desktop: *"no RPC layer, no worker, no tab leadership."*
4. **CSP.** `tauri.conf.json:22` is `default-src 'self'` — Web3Auth's popup/redirect flows and its network calls are not permitted under it today.

7. **The blueprints do not describe this sharing.** `packages/client` is never mentioned in `desktop.md`; `desktop` is never mentioned in `web-client.md`. There is no documented shared-JS story.

What already makes it cheaper than it looks:

- `useAuth.ts` — the actual orchestration — **touches zero browser APIs** and imports only `react`. Its state (mutex, restore latch) is already module-scoped `let`s outside React (`useAuth.ts:43-44`).

I have to correct something I told you, and it changes the shape of this.

**The identity change was decided, not accidental.** `blueprint/api.md:39-40` is explicit:

> Account = the Web3Auth-derived secp256k1 **identity key**; challenge-signature login; SIWE wallet login stays as a secondary auth method (feature-set decision FSM1/cipher-box-next#5).

I told you the identity provider moved and I could not find where that was decided. It is decided — in the frozen corpus (#5 for the method set, #28 D5 for the engine-owned token lifecycle), and restated in `engine.md`. v2 deliberately inverted v1's order. In v1 the API minted a JWT that produced the key; in v2 the key comes first from Web3Auth and the API authenticates it by challenge-signature. So SIWE genuinely cannot be a first login under the decided design, because there is no path from a wallet signature to a login secret. That is a real architectural decision, not wiring drift, and **#1253 as I filed it proposes undoing it**.

**What survives as a genuine defect** is narrower than I claimed: the Google client-ID conflation, which is unambiguous and unrelated to any of this.

**What is a real open question** is whether the decision should stand. That is yours to make, and the process for it is an ADR amending #5 — which is exactly what you proposed drafting.

**On your actual question, the evidence is one-sided:**

| | Share JS between hosts | Orchestrate in the engine |
|---|---|---|
| Desktop today | `frontend/` is a **43-line static HTML stub** — no JS, no bundler, no `dependencies`, no engine binding (`main.rs:3`: "Scaffold only: no engine wiring, no login") | Desktop links `crates/engine` natively (`desktop.md:21-24`) |
| Vehicle | None. `packages/client` is defined as web-side only, and `desktop.md:91-93` rules out its machinery — "no RPC layer, no worker, no tab leadership" | Already shared by construction: one engine, WASM on web, native link on desktop |
| Already built | Nothing | `login_identity`, `siwe_challenge/login/link`, single-flight `refresh`, `logout`, `test_login` — all in `api/client.rs:129-296` |

There is nothing to share JS *with*. A shared-orchestration package would mean first creating a desktop frontend, then parameterising over two different transports (WASM worker facade vs Tauri IPC commands that do not exist). And v1 tried the JS-sharing shape and did not achieve it — 3,600 lines against 2,400, duplicated, with measurable drift.

**So the ADR question is not "engine or shared JS".** It is: **should #5's method set be amended so a wallet can be a first login** — and if yes, that requires Core Kit to accept a CipherBox-issued JWT, which is v1's custom-verifier shape. Everything else is already decided and largely already built.

1. **Unlocking the Core Kit** — an identity provider vouches for the person, Core Kit returns the TSS key. v1 used a CipherBox-issued JWT against a custom verifier; v2 uses Web3Auth's own hosted OAuth.

# ADR 0008 — CipherBox issues the Core Kit identity token, and wallet login is first-class on web

- **Status:** Proposed
- **Date:** 2026-08-11
- **Amends:** [#5](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/5) — the clause "SIWE wallet
  login stays as a secondary auth method", restated in `blueprint/api.md` "Identity and auth"
- **Relates to:** [#28](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/28) D5 (the engine owns
  the token lifecycle; challenge-signature login) and
  [#34](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/34) (the auth method set and the
  per-platform `CredentialStore`), neither of which this decision changes
- **Implemented by:** [FSM1/cipher-box#1253](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/1253)

## Context

There are **two** authentications in a CipherBox login, and the v2 blueprint conflates them.

1. **Unlocking the Core Kit.** An identity provider vouches for the person; the Core Kit
   returns the TSS key the login secret derives from.
2. **Authenticating to the CipherBox API.** The engine signs a challenge with the derived
   identity key.

#28 D5 governs (2) and is correct as written. What was never decided is (1). v2 built it as
Web3Auth's own hosted OAuth; v1 built it as a CipherBox-issued JWT against a custom verifier.

The account model does not distinguish them, because it cannot: the Core Kit produces the same
key whichever provider vouched. So `blueprint/api.md`'s "Account = the Web3Auth-derived secp256k1
identity key" is true under both designs, and the choice of issuer was made in the client wiring
rather than in a decision.

### What the v2 choice costs

- **A wallet cannot be a first login.** SIWE authenticates an account; it cannot produce a login
  secret. So the wallet affordance on the cold login page dead-ends, and the refusal surfaces as
  "engine not started" — internal state, not anything the member can act on. `#938` proposes
  moving the affordance to a started-engine surface, which accommodates the limitation rather
  than removing it.
- **Passwordless email is delegated.** v1 owned it (`apps/api/src/auth/services/email-otp.service.ts`).
  v2 uses Web3Auth's `email_passwordless` sub-verifier, so the member's code delivery, its
  deliverability, its rate limits and its branding sit outside CipherBox.
- **The provider client ID was lost.** `subVerifierDetails.clientId` must be the OAuth provider's
  client ID; v2 passes the Web3Auth project client ID, so Google answers `401 invalid_client` for
  every attempt. `deploy-staging.yml` still supplies `VITE_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` and no v2 source
  reads it. This is a defect either way, not an argument about design.

### What v1 established about sharing

v1 shared **no** login code between its two hosts: roughly 3,600 lines in `apps/web` against
2,400 in `apps/desktop`, implementing the same flows twice. The shared boundary was drawn at the
bearer token — `packages/sdk` took `getAccessToken`, and everything that *produced* a token was
above the shared runtime and therefore per-host.

That boundary drifted, measurably:

- web mapped `production → MAINNET`, desktop mapped `production → DEVNET`;
- web carried a device-factor auto-recovery branch desktop lacked;
- web signed SIWE with `viem/siwe`, desktop hand-concatenated the EIP-4361 string;
- email OTP worked on web and broke in packaged desktop, because the JS half read a Vite
  compile-time variable and the Rust half read a runtime one, so two halves of one flow addressed
  two different API hosts.

Two facts bound how far sharing can go. The Core Kit **ran correctly in the Tauri webview** —
same SDK, same verifier, MFA and device approval functional — so it is not the obstacle. And
Google credential collection **cannot** be shared: Google Identity Services does not work in that
webview, the manual OAuth2 flow it falls back to needs a `redirect_uri`, and a packaged Tauri
origin is `tauri://localhost`, which Google rejects as a non-`http(s)` scheme. v1 solved it with a
loopback server on pre-registered ports.

Wallet access is the same kind of fact: the Tauri webview reaches no wallet. v1 wrote
`loginWithWallet` for desktop and never wired it — no UI trigger, never exercised.

## Decision

**D1 — CipherBox issues the identity token the Core Kit consumes.** Each verified method mints a
CipherBox JWT, and the Core Kit logs in against a CipherBox custom verifier via `loginWithJWT`,
with the API's own JWKS as the verification key. Passwordless email returns to the API, with its
delivery provider configured rather than assumed. Google keeps its own OAuth client ID, distinct
from the Web3Auth project client ID.

**D2 — Wallet login is a first-class first login, on web only.** This amends #5. A wallet signature
verified by the API mints the same CipherBox JWT as any other method, so it reaches the same
derived identity key and needs no separate account model. It is web-only because the Tauri webview
cannot reach a wallet — a platform property, not a deferred feature. Desktop offers the method set
minus wallet, and offers no affordance that cannot complete.

**D3 — One orchestration, host-specific credential collection.** The sequencing — provider
credential → API exchange → Core Kit login → secret export → `start(secret)` — lives in a single
host-agnostic package that both hosts import. Credential collection is injected per host.

The boundary is drawn at **credential collection**, one step earlier than v1 drew it. Everything
after that point converged on one path in v1 and drifted only because it was written twice.

### What this decision does not change

- The account is still the Web3Auth-derived secp256k1 identity key.
- Challenge-signature login to the API, the engine-held access JWT, and single-flight refresh
  (#28 D5) are untouched.
- The `CredentialStore` split stands: HTTP-only cookie on web, OS keychain on desktop (#34).
- The Core Kit still runs on the UI thread, owning its DOM and redirect flows, MFA enrollment and
  device approval.

## Alternatives rejected

**Keep Web3Auth's hosted OAuth and move the wallet affordance to a started-engine surface (#938).**
The smallest change, and it treats the symptom. It leaves a wallet unable to start a session at
all, leaves passwordless email delegated, and leaves the two client IDs conflated. #938's linked-
methods surface is still worth building; its premise is not.

**Move the orchestration into the engine.** Superficially the strongest option: the engine is
shared by construction, since desktop links `crates/engine` natively and web loads it as WASM, and
the engine already performs challenge-signature login, SIWE challenge/login/link, refresh and
logout. Rejected on two grounds. The Core Kit is a JS SDK that owns DOM and redirect flows, so it
cannot move; the engine would have to call back into the host for each step, and a new host seam
is a breaking change to `SeamSet`'s field-struct completeness gate and every implementor. And
under D1 the API exchange happens *before* a login secret exists, so the engine would additionally
need a command surface that works unstarted — today `command()` refuses everything pre-start. That
is more change for less gain than a shared package, and it can be revisited once the identity
phase is stable.

**Share through `packages/client`.** It is defined as one of the three web-side units, and its
whole non-type surface assumes Workers, `navigator.locks`, `BroadcastChannel`, Service Workers,
IndexedDB and OPFS. `blueprint/desktop.md` rules that machinery out on desktop — "no RPC layer,
no worker, no tab leadership".

**Draw the boundary at the bearer token, as v1 did.** Proven to drift, with the evidence listed
above.

## Consequences

1. **`blueprint/api.md`'s "Identity and auth" section changes**: CipherBox becomes the identity-token
   issuer, the wallet method becomes first-class and web-only, and the "secondary auth method"
   clause goes.
2. **`blueprint/web-client.md` and `blueprint/desktop.md` login sections** must name the shared
   orchestration package and state that credential collection is per-host. Neither file currently
   mentions the other's units.
3. **The API gains surface**: a JWKS endpoint, a JWT mint per verified method, and email OTP with a
   delivery provider. `siwe.service.ts` survives from v1 and is the starting point for the wallet
   half.
4. **Two client IDs must be configured and documented.** One environment variable for both is the
   defect above; the template that implies one is enough is how it recurs.
5. **Desktop needs a JS frontend.** `apps/desktop/frontend` is a 43-line static HTML file with no
   bundler, no TypeScript and no dependencies, and the shell links no engine. This is new build
   configuration, not a refactor, and it is the largest single cost of D3.
6. **A JWKS caching hazard is already on record** from v1, in exactly this handoff. Whoever
   implements D1 should read it before writing the verification path.
7. **The drift risk changes shape rather than disappearing.** One orchestration with two collectors
   still allows the collectors to diverge; what it removes is divergence in the sequencing, the
   verifier configuration, and the network map, which is where v1's drift actually occurred.

## Gate

- A member with no prior session signs in with a wallet on web and reaches a working vault.
- The same account signs in with Google on desktop and reaches the same vault. The wallet method is
  absent there, rather than present and unable to complete.
- Passwordless email is delivered by CipherBox, and a code it did not issue is refused.
- The Core Kit token is verified against CipherBox's JWKS; a token signed by anything else is
  refused.
- One implementation of the orchestration is imported by both hosts. The per-host code is
  credential collection and nothing else.
- A missing or wrong provider client ID fails naming which one, rather than surfacing a provider
  error the member cannot act on.

The blueprint and glossary are maintained in the `FSM1/cipher-box` repository. The `blueprint/`
copies in this repository are the as-charted archive and are not edited by this ADR.

A CipherBox login has **two** authentications, and the blueprint conflates them:

1. **Unlocking the Core Kit** — an identity provider vouches for the person; the Core Kit returns the TSS key.
2. **Authenticating to the API** — the engine signs a challenge with the derived identity key.

#28 D5 governs (2) and is correct as written. (1) was never decided. v2 built it as Web3Auth's hosted OAuth, in the client wiring; v1 had CipherBox mint a JWT against a custom verifier.

The account model cannot distinguish them, because the Core Kit yields the same key whichever provider vouched — so `blueprint/api.md`'s "Account = the Web3Auth-derived secp256k1 identity key" holds under both, and the issuer was chosen by accident rather than by decision.

Three decisions follow:

- **D1** — CipherBox issues the identity token the Core Kit consumes, via a custom verifier over its own JWKS. Passwordless email returns to the API. Google keeps its own OAuth client ID, distinct from the Web3Auth project one.
- **D2** — Wallet login is a first-class **first** login, **on web only**. This is the clause that amends #5. It is web-only because the Tauri webview reaches no wallet — a platform property, not a deferred feature.
- **D3** — One host-agnostic orchestration package; credential collection injected per host. The boundary is drawn at credential collection, one step earlier than v1 drew it.

Hand UAT on a local stack found all three login methods down, for three different reasons — one of which (Google answering `401 invalid_client`, because the Web3Auth project client ID is passed where the provider's belongs) is a plain defect that holds regardless of this ADR.

## Evidence it rests on

- v1 shared **no** login code across hosts: ~3,600 lines in `apps/web` against ~2,400 in `apps/desktop`, implementing the same flows twice. The shared boundary sat at `getAccessToken`, so everything producing a token was per-host by construction.
- That boundary drifted measurably: `MAINNET` vs `DEVNET` for the same environment, a device-factor recovery branch on one host only, `viem/siwe` against a hand-concatenated EIP-4361 string, and an email-OTP failure where the JS half read a compile-time API URL and the Rust half a runtime one.
- The Core Kit itself ran correctly in the Tauri webview, so it is not the obstacle.
- Google credential collection genuinely cannot be shared: GIS does not work in that webview, the fallback flow needs a `redirect_uri`, and a packaged Tauri origin is `tauri://localhost`, which Google rejects.
- v1 wrote desktop `loginWithWallet` and never wired it.

## Cost to be honest about

`apps/desktop/frontend` is a 43-line static HTML file with no bundler, no TypeScript and no dependencies, and the shell links no engine. D3 needs a desktop JS app to exist first. That is new build configuration, not a refactor, and it is the largest single cost here.

## Rejected, with reasons in the ADR

Moving the orchestration into the engine — attractive, since the engine is shared by construction and already performs challenge-signature login, SIWE challenge/login/link, refresh and logout. Work is tracked as sub-issues of this one — this body carries no checkbox list.

## Correction to this issue's original framing

This issue was filed asserting that v2 had regressed from v1 by accident. That is wrong, and the correction matters for scoping.

A CipherBox login has **two** authentications:

1. **Unlocking the Core Kit** — an identity provider vouches for the person; the Core Kit returns the TSS key the login secret derives from.
2. **Authenticating to the API** — the engine signs a challenge with the derived identity key.

(2) was decided — FSM1/cipher-box-next#28 D5, restated in `blueprint/engine.md` and `blueprint/api.md`. It is correct and nothing here changes it.

(1) was never decided. v2 built it as Web3Auth's hosted OAuth in the client wiring; v1 had CipherBox mint a JWT against a custom verifier. The account model cannot distinguish them, because the Core Kit yields the same secp256k1 key whichever provider vouched — so `blueprint/api.md`'s "Account = the Web3Auth-derived identity key" holds under both, and the issuer was chosen rather than decided.

ADR 0008 decides it. That makes the change far smaller than "restore v1": the account model, challenge-signature login, the engine-held token lifecycle, and the `CredentialStore` split all stand.

## What the ADR decides

- **D1** — CipherBox issues the identity token the Core Kit consumes, via a custom verifier over the API's own JWKS. Passwordless email returns to the API. Google's OAuth client ID is the provider's, distinct from the Web3Auth project client ID.
- **D2** — Wallet is a first-class **first** login, **web only**. This amends FSM1/cipher-box-next#5. It is web-only because the Tauri webview reaches no wallet — a platform property, not a deferred feature. v1 wrote that desktop path and never wired it.
- **D3** — One host-agnostic orchestration package; credential collection injected per host. The boundary sits at credential collection, one step earlier than v1 drew it at the bearer token, which is where v1's two hosts drifted.

## Why the boundary moved

v1 shared no login code: roughly 3,600 lines in `apps/web` against 2,400 in `apps/desktop`, implementing the same flows twice, and it drifted measurably — `MAINNET` against `DEVNET` for one environment, a device-factor recovery branch on one host only, `viem/siwe` against a hand-concatenated EIP-4361 string, and an email-OTP failure where one half read a compile-time API URL and the other a runtime one.

The Core Kit itself ran correctly in the Tauri webview, so it is not the obstacle. Exactly one step cannot be shared: Google credential collection, because GIS does not run in that webview and a packaged Tauri origin cannot satisfy the `redirect_uri` its fallback needs.

## Sequencing

#1256 is independent of the ADR and should land first — it is a live defect that breaks every Google sign-in today, whatever the identity architecture turns out to be.

The rest are provisional on FSM1/cipher-box-next#64 being accepted, and carry dependency edges rather than an order in prose.

`apps/web/src/auth/coreKit.ts` sources one value and spends it on two unrelated things:

The boundary sits at **credential collection**, one step earlier than v1 drew it at the bearer token. v1's `packages/sdk` took `getAccessToken` and was a pure token consumer, so everything that produced a token was per-host — roughly 3,600 lines in web against 2,400 in desktop, which drifted: `MAINNET` against `DEVNET` for one environment, a device-factor recovery branch on one host only, `viem/siwe` against a hand-concatenated EIP-4361 string, and an email-OTP failure where one half read a compile-time API URL and the other a runtime one.

## Why this is cheaper than it sounds

The orchestration is already isolated. `apps/web/src/auth/useAuth.ts` is 171 lines that **touch no browser API** and import only `react`; its mutex and restore latch are already module-scoped outside React. The SDK already sits behind the `CoreKitSession` seam (`coreKit.ts:20-31`), which tests substitute with a plain object.

## Work

- A new workspace package holding the sequencing: provider credential → API exchange → Core Kit login → secret export → `start(secret)`. `pnpm-workspace.yaml` already globs `packages/*`, so no workspace edit.
- Credential collection becomes an injected interface. Web supplies the Google popup and wagmi; desktop supplies its own.
- The package is parameterised over the facade it starts, since the transport differs per host — a WASM worker facade on web, Tauri IPC on desktop.
- `apps/web` imports it rather than owning it.

## Not `packages/client`

That package is defined as one of the three **web-side** units, and its non-type surface assumes Workers, `navigator.locks`, `BroadcastChannel`, Service Workers, IndexedDB and OPFS. `blueprint/desktop.md` rules that machinery out on desktop — "no RPC layer, no worker, no tab leadership".

## Acceptance

- One implementation of the sequencing, imported by `apps/web`.
- The package imports no browser API and no React.
- Web's behaviour is unchanged, proven by the existing auth tests.

**#1253 is now the ADR 0008 umbrella** — retitled, rewritten, and decomposed into six sub-issues with dependency edges.

| Issue | Layer | Blocked by |
|---|---|---|
| **#1256** Google client ID split | web | — **ship first** |

Three start immediately: **#1256**, **#1257**, **#1259**. I also made **#938 blocked by #1260**, since its premise dissolves once wallet can start a session — though I noted in #1260 that #938's linked-methods surface is still worth building, because *linking* a wallet to an existing account is a different intent from *logging in* with one.

Anyone picking this up needs that, or they will scope a rewrite instead of an issuer change.

All three are ready to merge, and checking them turned up a real problem.

| PR | ADR | Status now | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| **#62** | 0007 — derived first-run mint | `Proposed — not implemented` | none needed — verified accurate |
| **#63** | 0006 — owner-local sealed store | `Implemented` | updated, it had gone stale |
| **#64** | 0008 — identity token issuer | `Accepted — not implemented` | marked accepted |

**#63 had drifted while it sat open.** It said the contact-book and invite-record consumers were "not yet migrated" — but #1234 merged in the meantime, so all three stores now sit on the structure. I also split the implemented-by block, because #1207 (contact book) is closed while #1165 is not: the invite store is built and sealed but has no production caller, since `CreateInviteLink` has no mint path.

**#62 needed no edit** — I confirmed rather than assumed. Neither `genesis-read-scope-seed` nor `genesis-write-scope-seed` exists anywhere in `crates/`, and the KDF catalog still shows `owner-pointer-seed` with no genesis rows beside it.

**But #1220 was wrongly closed, and I have reopened it.** This is the one that matters. #1219's body contains the sentence **"It does not close #1220"** — and GitHub's linked-issue parser honours the closing keyword regardless of the negation in front of it, so the merge closed the issue two seconds later. The same trap closed #1016 earlier in this build.

It matters here because a closed #1220 makes ADR 0007 look partly moot, when in fact nothing was fixed. #1219 landed a positive vacancy precondition, and its own security review recorded why that is insufficient: an endpoint's `Ok(None)` is a **lookup miss, not an authoritative absence** — the endpoints are DHT-backed delegated routers and both host seams map 404 to `Ok(None)`. Unanimity defends against endpoints that *fail*, not against a live endpoint answering "no record" for a name a partitioned peer holds. The consequence stands: a second genesis mint destroys the only copy of a non-re-derivable write scope seed.

So all three issues ADR 0007 subsumes — #1220, #1221, #1222 — are open and unfixed, which is the state its rationale assumes.

Once #64 merges, **#1255** (the blueprint statement) can flip from draft to ready.
since ADR0007 is already scoped out I think its status should still be accepted.

content.text:
**No — it is not in ADR 0008's scope, and none of it exists in v2.** And there is a gap worth acting on.

**What v2 has:** exactly one thing. `coreKit.ts:66-71` detects `REQUIRED_SHARE` after login and refuses:

> MFA is on and this device holds no factor. Recovery and device approval are not built yet, so fail rather than half-log-in

It then logs out, clears the store, and throws. That is the *entire* v2 surface — the only mention of MFA or device approval in `apps/api/src`, `apps/web/src`, or `crates/`. No API endpoints (`auth.controller.ts` has challenge, login, siwe ×3, refresh, logout, test-login — nothing else), no engine surface, no UI.

**What v1 had was substantial**, and the API half is the part that gets overlooked:

- A whole API module — `device-approval/{controller,service,entity,module}`, two DTOs, and its own migration `AddDeviceApprovals`
- Nine web components (`DeviceApprovalModal`, `DeviceWaitingScreen`, `MfaEnrollmentWizard`, `RecoveryPhraseGrid`, `AuthorizedDevices`, …)
- Three hooks — `useMfa`, `useDeviceApproval`, `useDeviceRegistrySync`
- `lib/device/identity.ts`, which minted an Ed25519 device keypair in IndexedDB wrapped under HKDF of the vault key
- Desktop equivalents: `requestDeviceApproval`, `pollApprovalStatus`, `cancelApprovalRequest`, `inputRecoveryPhrase`

**The blueprint assumes it exists without scoping it.** Four references treat it as settled — `web-client.md:192` and `desktop.md:246` say MFA and device approval are "chrome-side", `web-client.md:260` lists `/settings` as carrying "MFA/devices (Core Kit UX)", and `testing.md:318` reserves a staging-dispatch job for "real Core Kit login (MFA, device approval)". All four describe it as UI-side Core Kit UX.

**That framing is wrong, and it is why this fell through.** Device approval is not Core Kit UX. An existing device approving a new one needs a server-side rendezvous — a pending-request row, a poll, and a response — which is exactly why v1 built an API module with a table for it. Calling it "chrome-side" hid an API slice.

**And nothing tracks it.** A search across all issues, open and closed, for MFA, device approval, recovery phrase, or authorized devices returns **nothing**. So this is an untracked gap, not a deferred one — the kind that surfaces at the staging cutover when a real account has MFA enrolled and cannot sign in on a second device.

**My recommendation: keep it out of ADR 0008 and file it separately.** ADR 0008 is about which provider unlocks the Core Kit; this is about what happens after unlocking when the account has a factor policy. Folding it in would roughly double an already-six-issue umbrella. But it deserves its own issue now, and probably its own ADR, since "chrome-side" needs correcting in three blueprint files and the API surface needs deciding.

Want me to file it?
yeah create an additional ADR for this, a blueprint update PR referring the ADR, and an umbrella issue to track related work (again multiple components will be impacted I suspect).
This needs v1's protocol before I can write a credible decision. Launching that research now.
